questions.rationale: Technical analysts study price and volume history, so they do not need financial statements. Quantitative analysts may use fundamental data, but they process it statistically, for example with regression. Option B reverses this.

questions.stem: The S&P/TSX Composite reaches a new high. On the same day, declining stocks outnumber advancing stocks by two to one. What does this breadth reading suggest?

options.A: The rise is broad, because the index level sets the trend
options.B: Few stocks take part in the rise, so the market move is narrow
options.C: The index is now above the intrinsic value of its stocks
options.D: Trading volume on the exchange must have fallen that day

questions.rationale: Breadth, or the advance-decline measure, shows whether many stocks join a market move. Here most stocks fell while the index rose, so a few large stocks drove the gain. Breadth does not measure intrinsic value.

questions.stem: Two analysts value Tregaron Pipelines Inc. with a discounted cash flow model and the same cash flow forecasts. One uses a discount rate of 8%, and the other uses 10%. What result is most likely?

options.A: Both find the same value, because the cash flow forecasts are identical
options.B: The analyst who uses 10% finds a higher value, because the rate measures growth
options.C: The analyst who uses 10% finds a lower value, because DCF depends on the discount rate
options.D: The values differ only slightly, because the rate affects only the final year

questions.rationale: A DCF value is the present value of expected future cash flows. So it depends heavily on the forecasts and on the discount rate. A higher rate lowers present values, so the analyst who uses 10% finds a lower value.

questions.stem: For which company is the constant-growth dividend discount model most suitable?

options.A: A software start-up that pays no dividends and reinvests all its cash
options.B: A mining company whose dividend changes sharply with metal prices
options.C: A biotech company that expects its first profit in five years
options.D: A mature utility that has raised its dividend steadily for decades

questions.rationale: The constant-growth dividend discount model assumes steady dividend growth below the required return. So it suits mature dividend payers such as a utility. A company with no dividend or a volatile dividend breaks the model's assumptions.

questions.stem: Client Tobias Mwangi sees that Ashcombe Software Inc. trades at a P/E of 20, against a peer average of 32. Valuations look stretched across the whole sector. What is the main weakness of calling Ashcombe cheap?

options.A: P/E ratios cannot be compared between companies in the same sector
options.B: A lower P/E always shows that a company's earnings are falling
options.C: Relative valuation assumes that the peers are fairly priced, which may be false
options.D: Relative valuation ignores the company's current share price

questions.rationale: Relative valuation compares P/E or price-to-book with peers, and it assumes that the peer group is fairly priced. If the whole sector is overvalued, a stock that is cheap against its peers can still be expensive. Comparison within a sector is normally correct.

questions.stem: A fundamental analysis says that Braemore Foods Inc. trades 25% below intrinsic value. But its price trend is down, and its latest filing is three months old. How should RR Ilse Varga use this for a client?

options.A: Find why the methods disagree, check for recent news, and explain the timing risk
options.B: Buy at once, because fundamental value always overrides the market's view
options.C: Ignore the fundamental view, because the price trend is the only current data
options.D: Wait for the next filing, because only financial statements are reliable

questions.rationale: No single source is complete: filings can be late, and market data shows only what investors do now. When methods disagree, find the reason before you act. Neither the fundamental view nor the trend alone decides the matter.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 4.11 importance of different sources

questions.stem: The economy enters a recession. Which company's earnings are most likely to fall the least?

options.A: A car manufacturer that sells mainly new vehicles
options.B: A maker of packaged food and household cleaning products
options.C: A cruise line that depends on holiday travel
options.D: A retailer of luxury clothing and jewellery

questions.rationale: Consumer staples, such as food and household goods, sell in good and bad times, so their earnings are defensive. Autos, travel and luxury retail are consumer discretionary. Their earnings follow income and confidence, so they are cyclical.

questions.stem: Hargrove Steel Corp. trades at a P/E of 5 after a record year at the top of the economic cycle. Client Nadia Petrakis calls it a bargain. What is the main risk?

options.A: A low P/E in a manufacturing company always shows accounting problems
options.B: The P/E is low because the company pays no dividends to shareholders
options.C: Steel companies have low fixed costs, so their profits cannot rise further
options.D: Peak-cycle earnings are likely to fall, so the low P/E can be a trap

questions.rationale: Manufacturing and materials companies have high fixed costs, so profits swing widely with sales. At the top of the cycle, earnings are temporarily high, so a low P/E can be a trap. Option C reverses the cost structure.

questions.stem: Why do analysts often value a bank with the price-to-book ratio?

options.A: A bank's assets are mainly financial, so their book value is meaningful
options.B: Banks pay no dividends, so dividend models do not apply to them
options.C: Bank earnings are too stable for the P/E ratio to be useful
options.D: Banks have no debt, so their book value equals their market value

questions.rationale: Analysts often value banks on price-to-book, because their assets are mainly financial. Banks commonly pay dividends and carry large liabilities, so options B and D are false. Stable earnings do not make the P/E ratio useless.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 4.12 service industries (banks on price-to-book)

questions.stem: Client Leontyne Abara holds utility shares for income. Why do investors often compare utility dividend yields with bond yields?

options.A: Utilities must pay dividends equal to the Government of Canada bond yield
options.B: Utility shares are a type of fixed-income security under securities law
options.C: Utilities pay high, steady dividends, so they compete with bonds for income investors
options.D: Utility earnings rise when interest rates rise, just as bond yields do

questions.rationale: Utilities have regulated, recurring revenue, high debt and high dividends. So income investors compare their yields with bond yields. When bond yields rise, utilities become less attractive, and their high debt costs more.

questions.stem: Velmont Semiconductor Inc. trades at a P/E of 45. It reports that sales growth slowed from 30% to 12%. Its shares fall 35%, though it is still profitable. What best explains the large drop?

options.A: The company must now pay a dividend, which lowers its value
options.B: Its high multiple reflected expected growth, so slower growth cuts the multiple fast
options.C: Technology companies must report under a different accounting standard
options.D: Its P/E is now negative, because its earnings growth slowed

questions.rationale: Investors pay high P/E multiples for the expected growth of technology companies. If growth slows, these multiples can fall fast, so the price drops more than earnings. Slower growth does not make a profitable company's P/E negative.

questions.stem: An industry has steady but slower growth. Its companies pay out a larger share of earnings as dividends, and their shares trade at moderate P/E multiples. Which life-cycle stage is it most likely in?

options.A: Growth
options.B: Introduction
options.C: Decline
options.D: Maturity

questions.rationale: In maturity, an industry has steady growth, a higher payout and a moderate multiple. The growth stage has fast growth and a low payout. Introduction has little or no profit, and decline has low growth and a low multiple.

questions.stem: Economists expect the monthly CPI report to show annual inflation of 3.1%. The report shows exactly 3.1%, up from 2.6% last month. Bond and stock prices barely move. Why?

options.A: Inflation affects bond prices, but it never affects stock prices
options.B: Markets react only to employment data, not to inflation data
options.C: The result matched the consensus, so prices already reflected it
options.D: A rise in inflation always pushes bond and stock prices up together

questions.rationale: Markets price expectations. A surprise against the consensus forecast moves prices, not the news alone. Here the report matched the forecast, so prices had already adjusted. Inflation can affect both bonds and stocks.

questions.stem: The central bank raises its policy rate by more than economists expected. Which of these holdings will most likely fall the most in price?

options.A: A 90-day Government of Canada treasury bill
options.B: A money market fund that holds short-term deposits
options.C: A grocery chain with steady current earnings and no debt
options.D: A software firm that expects most profits more than ten years from now

questions.rationale: A higher rate makes future cash flows worth less today, so stocks with distant earnings react most. Short-term instruments barely change in price. A debt-free grocer with current earnings is less sensitive to the discount rate.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 4.13 interest rates (distant earnings react most)

questions.stem: Inflation rises sharply, and input costs climb across the economy. Which company is best placed to protect its profit margins?

options.A: A manufacturer that sells a commodity at fixed long-term contract prices
options.B: A company with a strong brand that can raise prices without losing customers
options.C: An airline that cannot pass higher fuel costs on to its customers
options.D: A builder that agreed fixed prices on projects that end in three years

questions.rationale: When inflation rises, input costs rise. Companies with pricing power can raise their prices, so they protect their margins better than others. Fixed contract prices or weak pricing power leave margins exposed to the higher costs.

questions.stem: Client Anouk Dessaline holds a bond with a fixed 5% coupon. Over the year, inflation rises from 2% to 4%. What happens to the real return from her coupon?

options.A: It falls, because inflation lowers the real value of fixed coupons
options.B: It rises, because higher inflation raises the coupon payments
options.C: It stays the same, because the coupon rate does not change
options.D: It rises, because bond prices go up when inflation rises

questions.rationale: Real return is about equal to the nominal return minus inflation. Her coupon is fixed, so higher inflation lowers its real value, from about 3% to about 1%. Rising inflation usually pushes yields up and bond prices down.

questions.stem: GDP has grown for two quarters after a recession, but the unemployment rate still rises. Client Ewan Halvorsen says that the recession must be getting worse. What should his RR explain?

options.A: Rising unemployment always shows that a new recession has started
options.B: Unemployment is a leading indicator, so GDP will soon fall again
options.C: Unemployment is a lagging indicator, and it often rises after a recovery starts
options.D: GDP data is unreliable, so only employment data shows the cycle

questions.rationale: Unemployment is a lagging indicator. It often continues to rise after a recovery starts. Option B wrongly calls it a leading indicator. Leading indicators, such as stock prices, turn before the economy.

questions.stem: Consumer spending and wage growth both come in far above economists' forecasts. That day, bond yields jump and stock indices fall. What best explains the fall in stocks?

options.A: Strong consumer spending always lowers company earnings
options.B: Investors now expect the central bank to raise rates, which lowers valuations
options.C: Higher wages always reduce productivity, so earnings will fall
options.D: Stock prices fall whenever data differs from the forecast, in either direction

questions.rationale: Strong spending supports earnings, but fast wage growth adds to inflation pressure. Investors expect rate hikes, and higher rates lower valuations. Here the rate effect outweighs the earnings effect, so good economic news pushes stocks down.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 4.13 exam trap (good news, rate expectations)

questions.stem: Client Priyanka Rasmussen needs $40,000 for tuition in 12 months. She wants to hold it in equities, because stocks have averaged about 9% a year. What is the best response?

options.A: Equities suit her, because their long-run average applies to any horizon
options.B: Equities suit her if she picks a fund with a low management fee
options.C: A balanced fund is ideal, because its bonds remove the risk of a loss
options.D: Cash or short-term bonds suit her, because one-year equity results include large losses

questions.rationale: One-year equity outcomes are widely spread, including large losses. A short-horizon investor cannot expect the long-run average return of equities. Money needed within a year or two usually belongs in cash or short-term bonds.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 4.14 volatility and exam trap

questions.stem: Client Lorcan Abernethy reads that equities become less risky the longer you hold them. Which statement about a longer holding period is correct?

options.A: The spread of average annual returns narrows, but the range of final dollar wealth does not
options.B: The range of final dollar wealth narrows, and so does the spread of annual returns
options.C: Both spreads stay the same, because volatility does not depend on the horizon
options.D: The spread of average annual returns widens, while final wealth becomes certain

questions.rationale: Over long horizons, the spread of average annual returns narrows. But the range of final dollar wealth does not narrow. So a long horizon reduces uncertainty about the average return, not about the final dollar amount.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 4.14 volatility (average annual returns vs final wealth)

questions.stem: The economy moves from a trough into recovery. Which sectors usually lead the market in this phase?

options.A: Consumer staples and utilities, because their earnings are defensive
options.B: Real estate and utilities, because they pay regular income
options.C: Cyclical sectors, such as consumer discretionary and industrials
options.D: Health care services, because demand for them stays fixed

questions.rationale: Over months, sector leadership rotates through the cycle. Cyclical sectors lead in recoveries, because their earnings follow the economy. Defensive sectors, such as staples and utilities, stand out mainly by losing less in downturns.

questions.stem: Which pair are leading economic indicators that tend to turn before the economy does?

options.A: The unemployment rate and stock prices
options.B: Stock prices and building permits
options.C: The unemployment rate and building permits
options.D: Last quarter's GDP and the unemployment rate

questions.rationale: Leading indicators, such as stock prices and building permits, turn before the economy. Lagging indicators, such as unemployment, turn after it. So every pair that includes the unemployment rate is wrong.

questions.stem: Client Odalys Brennan holds an energy-sector fund. In one quarter, oil prices drop, and the fund falls 12% while the broad market falls 3%. The energy sector index falls 11%. She wants to sell. What is the best assessment?

options.A: The fund did about as well as its sector, so judge it against that benchmark over a full cycle
options.B: The fund failed, because it trailed the broad market by 9 points in one quarter
options.C: The fund outperformed, because it fell less than the broad market
options.D: The fund should track the broad market, so its manager took too much risk

questions.rationale: A sector fund can differ widely from the broad market in the short term. Against its sector benchmark, this fund did about as expected. Over a quarter, results can differ by chance, so judge performance over a full cycle.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 4.14 benchmarks and market sector; -12 vs -11 sector, -3 market

questions.stem: Under securities law, which feature makes an investment fund a mutual fund, and not a non-redeemable investment fund?

options.A: Its securities give the holder a right to redeem on demand at an amount based on net assets.
options.B: Its securities trade on a stock exchange at a price that supply and demand set.
options.C: It invests money from many investors under the direction of a professional manager.
options.D: It distributes all of its net income and net capital gains to investors each year.

questions.rationale: A mutual fund's securities entitle the holder to receive, on demand, an amount based on the fund's net assets. A non-redeemable investment fund also pools investor money under a manager. So pooling does not separate the two, but the redemption right does.
questions.source_quote: "“mutual fund” means an issuer whose primary purpose is to invest money provided by its security holders and whose securities entitle the holder to receive on demand, or within a specified period after demand, an amount computed by reference to the value of a proportionate interest" — research/sources/gov/ontario-securities-act-extracts.txt Securities Act (Ontario) s.1(1) 'mutual fund', ~L180

questions.stem: A closed-end fund and an ETF both trade on a stock exchange. Why can the closed-end fund trade at a persistent discount to NAV, while the ETF usually does not?

options.A: The ETF must calculate its NAV each hour, but the closed-end fund calculates it once a year.
options.B: The closed-end fund must hold only illiquid assets, but the ETF must hold only index securities.
options.C: The ETF has a creation and redemption process that lets authorized dealers keep its price near NAV.
options.D: The closed-end fund cannot pay distributions, but the ETF must pay distributions each month.

questions.rationale: Only an ETF has a creation and redemption process. Authorized dealers use it for arbitrage when the price moves away from NAV. A closed-end fund issues units mainly at its IPO, so supply does not adjust and a discount can persist.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 5.1 exam trap and 5.5 creation and redemption

questions.stem: Priya buys shares of a mutual fund corporation in a non-registered account. Which tax slip does she receive for the fund's distributions?

options.A: A T3 slip, because the fund passes its income through to her as a trust
options.B: A T5 slip, because the corporation pays dividends and capital gains dividends
options.C: No slip, because the corporation pays the tax on all income inside the fund
options.D: Both a T3 slip and a T5 slip, because she holds both units and shares

questions.rationale: A mutual fund corporation issues shares and pays dividends and capital gains dividends, which it reports on a T5 slip. A mutual fund trust issues units and gives a T3 slip. Priya holds shares of a corporation, so the T3 answer is wrong.
rule_refs: CRA Tax treatment of mutual funds
questions.source_quote: "If you own units of a mutual fund trust, the trust will give you a T3 slip, Statement of Trust Income Allocations and Designations. If you own shares of a mutual fund corporation, the corporation will give you a T5 slip" — research/sources/cra/capital-gains-losses-superficial-loss-pages.txt CRA 'Tax treatment of mutual funds' — How income is taxed, ~L1604

questions.stem: A conventional mutual fund holds 9% of its NAV in securities of one issuer. The portfolio manager wants to buy more, which would take the position to 12% of NAV. For which issuer is this purchase permitted?

options.A: A Canadian chartered bank, through its common shares
options.B: A utility company, through its senior bonds
options.C: A mining company, through its preferred shares
options.D: The Government of Canada, through its bonds

questions.rationale: A conventional mutual fund must not buy a security if more than 10% of its NAV would then be in one issuer. The limit does not apply to a government security. A corporate bond is still a security of one issuer, so the utility purchase breaks the limit.
questions.source_quote: "(a) a government security;" — research/sources/csa/ni-81-102-investment-funds.txt NI 81-102 s.2.1(2)(a), ~L1050

questions.stem: Malik holds 75% of his account in one energy fund with 50 stocks. He asks his RR to buy more and says, "A fund is always diversified." Which assessment is most accurate?

options.A: The fund holds 50 stocks, so the account is diversified, and concentration is not a suitability factor here.
options.B: The fund obeys the 10% single-issuer limit, so the dealer may treat the whole account as diversified.
options.C: The fund spreads risk over many issuers, but the account is concentrated in one sector, and the dealer must consider this.
options.D: Concentration applies only to individual stocks, so the dealer may accept the order with no further review.

questions.rationale: A sector fund spreads money over many issuers, but one sector shock hits the whole holding. The single-issuer limit counts issuers, not sectors. Under IDPC 3402(1), the dealer must consider the concentration of securities in the account.
questions.source_quote: "the impact of the action on the retail client’s account, including the concentration of securities, derivatives or precious metals bullion, within the account and the liquidity of those securities, derivatives or precious metals bullion," — research/sources/ciro/idpc-rules-2026-08-11.txt IDPC 3402(1)(i)(c), ~L6803

questions.stem: Which statement about who holds a mutual fund's portfolio assets is correct?

options.A: A custodian holds them, and the manager must not act as custodian of the fund.
options.B: The manager holds them, because the manager directs the business of the fund.
options.C: The principal distributor holds them, because it sells the units of the fund.
options.D: Each participating dealer holds the assets that belong to its own clients.

questions.rationale: The portfolio assets are held under the custodianship of one custodian. NI 81-102 says that the manager must not act as custodian or sub-custodian. This split protects investors, because the firm that directs the fund does not also hold its assets.
questions.source_quote: "Despite any other provisions of this Part, the manager of an investment fund must not act as custodian or sub-custodian of the investment fund." — research/sources/csa/ni-81-102-part-6-custodianship-part-11-commingling-of-cash.txt NI 81-102 s.6.1(6), ~L84

questions.stem: Ravi places an order to buy units of a mutual fund on Tuesday, after the daily cut-off time. The fund treats late orders as received on the next business day. At which price does the fund fill his order?

options.A: The NAVPS that the fund calculated at the close on Monday
options.B: The NAVPS that the fund calculates at the close on Tuesday
options.C: The market price at the time that the fund receives the order
options.D: The NAVPS that the fund calculates at the close on Wednesday

questions.rationale: Under forward pricing, the fund uses the NAVPS next determined after it receives the order. The fund treats Ravi's late order as received on Wednesday, so Wednesday's NAVPS applies. Forward pricing stops investors from buying at a known, stale price.
questions.source_quote: "The issue price of a security of a mutual fund to which a purchase order pertains must be the net asset value per security of that class, or series of a class, next determined after the receipt by the mutual fund of the order." — research/sources/csa/ni-81-102-investment-funds.txt NI 81-102 s.9.3(1), ~L2408

questions.stem: A mutual fund uses specified derivatives to hedge its currency risk. Under NI 81-106, what is the minimum frequency at which it must calculate its NAV?

options.A: Once a week
options.B: Every business day
options.C: Once a month
options.D: At each quarter end

questions.rationale: NI 81-106 sets a weekly minimum for a fund that does not use specified derivatives or sell short. A fund that uses specified derivatives or sells short must calculate NAV every business day. The monthly exception applies only to the weekly minimum.
questions.source_quote: "(a) if the investment fund does not use specified derivatives or sell securities short, once a week; (b) if the investment fund uses specified derivatives or sells securities short, once every business day." — research/sources/csa/ni-81-106-investment-fund-continuous-disclosure-nav-mer.txt NI 81-106 s.14.2(3), ~L439

questions.stem: Under the NI 81-102 risk classification method, a mutual fund's 10-year annualized standard deviation is exactly 16.0%. Which risk level applies to the fund?

options.A: Medium
options.B: Medium to high
options.C: High
options.D: Low to medium

questions.rationale: The medium band is 11 to less than 16. The medium-to-high band is 16 to less than 20. A standard deviation of exactly 16.0% is therefore in the medium-to-high band, not the medium band.
questions.source_quote: "0 to less than 6 Low 6 to less than 11 Low to medium 11 to less than 16 Medium 16 to less than 20 Medium to high 20 or greater High" — research/sources/csa/ni-81-102-investment-funds.txt NI 81-102 Appendix F Item 1(1) table, ~L3655-3685

questions.stem: A new mutual fund has 3 years of returns. It is a clone fund, and its underlying fund has 12 years of history. The manager prefers to use a broad reference index for the missing years. What must the manager do?

options.A: Use the reference index, because the manager may choose any proxy.
options.B: Use only the 3 years of returns that the fund itself has earned.
options.C: Use the returns of the underlying fund for the missing 7 years.
options.D: Wait until the fund has 10 years of returns before it sets a level.

questions.rationale: A fund with less than 10 years of history fills the missing years from a proxy. A clone fund whose underlying fund has 10 years of history must use that fund's returns. A reference index applies only when no clone or matching fund exists.
questions.source_quote: "if the mutual fund is a clone fund and the underlying fund has 10 years of performance history," — research/sources/csa/ni-81-102-investment-funds.txt NI 81-102 Appendix F Item 4(1), ~L3776

questions.stem: Nadia sees a "Low" risk rating in a fund's Fund Facts. She tells her RR that the fund cannot lose money. Which reply is correct?

options.A: The rating reflects past volatility, and a low-rated fund can still lose money.
options.B: The rating guarantees that the fund will not fall in value over 10 years.
options.C: The rating measures the chance of loss, so a loss is very unlikely.
options.D: The rating is fixed at launch, so it shows the fund's future volatility.

questions.rationale: The risk level comes from the annualized standard deviation of past returns. Fund Facts must say that the rating does not show future volatility and that a low-rated fund can still lose money. The rating does not measure the chance of loss.
questions.source_quote: "It doesn’t tell you how volatile the fund will be in the future. The rating can change over time. A fund with a low risk rating can still lose money." — research/sources/csa/form-81-101f3-fund-facts.txt Form 81-101F3 Part I Item 4(2)(b), ~L395

questions.stem: During the day, an ETF's market price rises well above the NAV of its holdings. Which action by authorized dealers usually moves the price back toward NAV?

options.A: They buy units on the exchange and return them to the ETF in exchange for the basket.
options.B: They ask the manager to suspend trading in the ETF until its market price falls.
options.C: They ask the manager to calculate a new NAV for the ETF at a higher value.
options.D: They deliver a basket of securities for new units and sell those units on the exchange.

questions.rationale: When the price is above NAV, authorized dealers create units with a basket and sell them, which adds supply. Buying units and redeeming them is the correct action when the price is below NAV, not above it.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 5.5 creation and redemption, arbitrage

questions.stem: Oskar wants to buy a thinly traded ETF. He plans to place a market order two minutes after the market opens. Which advice best protects him from paying too much?

options.A: Use a market order, because a market order always fills at the ETF's NAV.
options.B: Check the average bid-ask spread, and use a limit order or trade later in the day.
options.C: Place the order after the close, so that it fills at the next calculated NAV.
options.D: Buy a larger number of units, because a larger order narrows the spread.

questions.rationale: Prices can be more volatile near the open, and a thin market has a wide spread. A market order fills at the best price available now, not at NAV. ETF Facts suggests a limit order or a trade at another time of day.
questions.source_quote: "Consider using a limit order or placing a trade at another time" — research/sources/csa/form-41-101f4-etf-facts.txt Form 41-101F4 Part I Item 6, ~L926

questions.stem: A conventional mutual fund receives unusually large redemption requests. Which cash borrowing is permitted for the fund?

options.A: A temporary loan of up to 5% of NAV to pay redemptions while it sells assets in an orderly way
options.B: A temporary loan of up to 50% of NAV from a lender that can act as a fund custodian
options.C: A permanent loan of up to 5% of NAV to buy more securities for the portfolio
options.D: A loan of up to 300% of NAV, if the fund also sells securities short

questions.rationale: A conventional mutual fund may borrow only as a temporary measure, to meet redemptions or settle trades. Its total borrowing must not exceed 5% of NAV. The 50% limit applies to alternative mutual funds and non-redeemable investment funds.
questions.source_quote: "the transaction is a temporary measure to accommodate requests for the redemption of securities of the investment fund while the investment fund effects an orderly liquidation of portfolio assets, or to permit the investment fund to settle portfolio transactions" — research/sources/csa/ni-81-102-investment-funds.txt NI 81-102 s.2.6(1)(a)(i), ~L1471

questions.stem: Which feature best describes a smart-beta ETF?

options.A: It weights securities by market capitalization, like a standard broad index.
options.B: Its manager selects securities freely to beat a benchmark each year.
options.C: It follows rules that weight securities by factors such as value or low volatility.
options.D: It uses swaps to deliver twice the daily return of an index.

questions.rationale: A smart-beta index follows rules, like a passive index, but it weights securities by factors, not by market capitalization. An active manager selects securities freely. A fund that seeks a multiple of the daily return is a leveraged fund.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 5.6 smart beta and factor investing

questions.stem: Lena tells her dealer that her mutual fund purchase must be completed immediately. Delivery of the Fund Facts before then is not reasonably practicable. What else must the dealer do before it accepts the order?

options.A: Get her blanket written consent to later delivery of Fund Facts for all of her future purchases.
options.B: Deliver the simplified prospectus at once, because it replaces the Fund Facts for urgent orders.
options.C: Explain the Fund Facts, get her consent to later delivery for this purchase, and give a verbal summary.
options.D: Nothing more, because an urgent instruction from the client removes the Fund Facts delivery rule.

questions.rationale: The urgent-purchase exception needs more than the client's instruction. Before it accepts the order, the dealer explains Fund Facts and its delivery duty. It gets consent for that specific purchase and gives a verbal summary. A blanket consent is not valid.
questions.source_quote: "the purchaser instructs the dealer that the purchase must be completed immediately or by a specified time;" — research/sources/csa/ni-81-101-mutual-fund-prospectus-disclosure.txt NI 81-101 s.3.2.02(1)(a), ~L1362

questions.stem: Thea added a large sum to a fund just before the market fell. Her annual report shows a return well below the fund's published return. Which statement best explains the gap?

options.A: Her report uses a time-weighted return, which removes the effect of her cash flows.
options.B: The fund's published return includes sales charges, but her own return excludes them.
options.C: The manager's poor decisions affected her units more than the units of other investors.
options.D: Her report uses a money-weighted return, which reflects the timing of her cash flows.

questions.rationale: A money-weighted return depends on the timing and size of deposits, so money added before a decline lowers it. The fund's published return is time-weighted, and cash flows do not affect it. Published returns also exclude sales charges.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 5.8 MWRR vs TWRR and exam trap

questions.stem: A rating service compares a fund with the average of its peer group. Some funds in the group closed during the period and dropped out of the data. Which problem does this cause?

options.A: Style drift, because the fund moved away from its stated investment style
options.B: Survivorship bias, because only the surviving funds remain in the average
options.C: Tracking difference, because the fund's return differed from its index return
options.D: Concentration, because the peer group now holds too few funds to compare

questions.rationale: Closed or merged funds drop out of the data, so only survivors remain, and their average looks too good. Style drift is a different problem: a fund moves away from its stated style, so its peers no longer match it.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 5.8 peer group, survivorship bias

questions.stem: The Larchmont Income Fund has total assets of $82,400,000 and total liabilities of $1,400,000. It has 6,000,000 units outstanding. What is its NAVPS?
questions.rationale: NAVPS = (total assets - total liabilities) / units outstanding = (82,400,000 - 1,400,000) / 6,000,000 = $13.50. The $13.73 answer ignores the liabilities, and the $13.97 answer adds them.

questions.stem: Wren invests $25,000 in a mutual fund. She pays a 4% front-end sales charge, which the dealer deducts from the amount invested. The NAVPS is $16.00. How many units does she receive?
questions.rationale: The charge is 0.04 x 25,000 = $1,000, so the net amount invested is $24,000. Units issued = 24,000 / 16.00 = 1,500. The 1,562.50 answer ignores the sales charge.

questions.stem: One year ago, a fund's NAVPS was $15.00. Today it is $15.90, after cash distributions of $0.60 per unit. What is the fund's total return per unit for the year?
questions.rationale: Total return = (ending NAVPS - beginning NAVPS + distributions) / beginning NAVPS = (15.90 - 15.00 + 0.60) / 15.00 = 10.0%. The 6.0% answer ignores the distributions, and 9.4% wrongly divides by the ending NAVPS.

questions.stem: Dmitri held 800 units of a fund one year ago at a NAVPS of $25.00. Today the NAVPS is $26.00, after cash distributions of $0.75 per unit. The fund's benchmark returned 8.5%. Which statement is correct?

options.A: His holding is worth $20,800, and the fund beat its benchmark by 1.5 percentage points.
options.B: His holding is worth $20,800, and the fund lagged its benchmark by 1.5 percentage points.
options.C: His holding is worth $21,400, and the fund lagged its benchmark by 1.5 percentage points.
options.D: His holding is worth $20,800, and the fund lagged its benchmark by 4.5 percentage points.

questions.rationale: Value = 800 x 26.00 = $20,800, because the distributions were paid in cash. Total return = (26.00 - 25.00 + 0.75) / 25.00 = 7.0%. This is 1.5 points below the 8.5% benchmark. The 4.5 answer ignores the distributions.

questions.stem: Which cost is excluded from a mutual fund's MER and shown instead in its trading expense ratio (TER)?

options.A: The trailing commission that the fund pays to the client's dealer
options.B: The management fee that the fund pays to the fund manager
options.C: Commissions that the fund pays to buy and sell its portfolio securities
options.D: The legal, audit and other operating expenses of the fund

questions.rationale: The MER covers the management fee, including any trailing commission, plus operating expenses. The fund's trading costs, such as commissions on portfolio trades, are excluded from the MER and appear in the TER.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 5.10 MER and TER table

questions.stem: Kofi holds a Canadian-listed ETF of U.S. dividend stocks in his TFSA. The ETF is a trust, and U.S. tax is withheld on the dividends. What is true about this withholding tax?

options.A: It is unrecoverable, because he does not report the income and so has no foreign tax credit.
options.B: It is recoverable, because the trust passes the foreign tax through to him on a T3 slip.
options.C: It is recoverable, because the tax treaty exempts all registered plans from U.S. tax.
options.D: It does not apply, because U.S. law exempts every TFSA from withholding tax on dividends.

questions.rationale: Income in a TFSA is generally tax-free, so Kofi does not report the foreign income on his return. Without reported income, he cannot claim a foreign tax credit. The T3 pass-through helps only in a non-registered account.
questions.source_quote: "any income you earn through interest, dividends or capital gains are generally tax-free" — research/sources/cra/tfsa-pages.txt CRA 'What is a TFSA', ~L167

questions.stem: Sana holds a mutual fund in a non-registered account and reinvests all distributions in new units. How are the distributions taxed?

options.A: They are tax-free, because she did not receive any cash from the fund.
options.B: They are taxable only when she redeems the new units that she received.
options.C: They reduce her ACB, so the tax is deferred until she sells her units.
options.D: They are taxable in the year she receives them, as if she had received cash.

questions.rationale: In a non-registered account, distributions are taxable whether she gets them in cash or reinvests them. The CRA considers that she received the amounts before the reinvestment. Only a return of capital reduces the ACB.
rule_refs: CRA Tax treatment of mutual funds
questions.source_quote: "Keep in mind that if you hold your fund in a non-registered account, fund distributions are included in your taxable income, whether you get them in cash or have them reinvested." — research/sources/csa/form-81-101f3-fund-facts.txt Form 81-101F3 Part I Item 8, ~L695

questions.stem: Yusuf holds T-series units of a mutual fund trust in a non-registered account. Return of capital has already reduced his ACB to zero. This year he receives another $900 of return of capital. What is the tax effect?

options.A: The $900 is not taxed now, and his ACB becomes negative $900.
options.B: The $900 is taxed as interest income, and his ACB stays at zero.
options.C: The $900 is a deemed capital gain this year, and his ACB stays at zero.
options.D: The $900 is not taxed now, and he pays tax on it only at a sale.

questions.rationale: Return of capital reduces the ACB and defers tax. For mutual fund trust units, an ACB below zero gives a deemed capital gain in the year. The ACB then resets to zero, so the tax is not deferred to the sale.
rule_refs: CRA Tax treatment of mutual funds
questions.source_quote: "If the ACB of the units of the trust is reduced below zero during the tax year, the negative amount is deemed to be a capital gain in the year." — research/sources/cra/capital-gains-losses-superficial-loss-pages.txt CRA 'Tax treatment of mutual funds', ~L1696

questions.stem: A conventional mutual fund holds 45% of its assets in securities listed on one foreign exchange. That exchange halts all trading for two days, and no other market trades the securities. The fund has no regulatory approval. May it suspend redemptions?

options.A: Yes, because any exchange halt lets a mutual fund suspend redemptions.
options.B: No, because the halted exchange lists less than 50% of the fund's assets.
options.C: Yes, if the fund continues to accept purchases during the suspension.
options.D: No, because a mutual fund may never suspend redemptions for any reason.

questions.rationale: Without approval, a mutual fund may suspend redemptions if trading halts on an exchange that lists more than 50% of its assets. No practical alternative market must exist. At 45%, that condition fails. A permitted suspension also bars new purchases.
questions.source_quote: "represent more than 50% by value, or underlying market exposure, of the total assets of the investment fund without allowance for liabilities and if those securities or specified derivatives are not traded on any other exchange that represents a reasonably practical alternative" — research/sources/csa/ni-81-102-investment-funds.txt NI 81-102 s.10.6(1)(a), ~L2774

questions.stem: Ama sets up a monthly withdrawal plan from her mutual funds with her Registered Individual. Under CIRO guidance, when should a suitability determination take place?

options.A: When the plan is established, and when a triggering event occurs
options.B: Before each monthly withdrawal that the plan makes from her funds
options.C: Only at the annual account review, and not when the plan starts
options.D: At no time, because planned withdrawals are outside the suitability rule

questions.rationale: CIRO guidance says planned withdrawals need no suitability determination before each withdrawal. The Registered Individual should make one before the plan starts and when a triggering event occurs. So a review before each monthly payment is not required.
questions.source_quote: "Pre-authorized purchases or withdrawals pursuant to established plans do not require a suitability determination before each purchase or withdrawal. However, a Registered Individual should make a suitability determination before establishing a plan and when a triggering event occurs." — research/sources/ciro/gn-3400-21-004-kyc-suitability-retail-clients.txt GN-3400-21-004, ~L634

questions.stem: Ines has $8,000 to invest and can add $150 each month. She has little time or investment knowledge. Which choice is most likely suitable for her?

options.A: Three bank stocks, with a commission on each monthly purchase
options.B: A single sector fund that holds only technology stocks
options.C: An ETF bought each month, with a commission on each $150 trade
options.D: A diversified mutual fund with a pre-authorized monthly purchase plan

questions.rationale: Her small amounts cannot buy a diversified portfolio of stocks at a low cost. A diversified fund gives diversification and professional management. Small automatic purchases cost nothing extra in a mutual fund, but each ETF trade has a commission and a spread.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 5.12 investor decisions and RR recommendation

questions.stem: Felix has $2 million in a non-registered account, all in high-MER equity funds. He follows markets closely and wants to decide when to realize capital gains. Which recommendation best puts his interest first?

options.A: Keep the funds, because a large account gains the most from pooled management and fees.
options.B: Consider direct holdings or a managed account, and weigh the tax cost of selling the funds.
options.C: Switch to other high-MER funds that pay a higher trailing commission to the dealer.
options.D: Sell all the funds at once, because tax costs are not a factor in a recommendation.

questions.rationale: The MERs apply to his whole $2 million each year, so costs have a large impact on his returns. Direct holdings give him control of trades and of the timing of gains. The dealer must consider costs and a reasonable range of alternatives.
questions.source_quote: "the potential and actual impact of costs on the retail client’s returns, and" — research/sources/ciro/idpc-rules-2026-08-11.txt IDPC 3402(1)(i)(d), ~L6806

questions.stem: Which statement about a principal-protected note (PPN) that a bank issues is correct?

options.A: It pays a fixed rate of interest each year, whatever the index does.
options.B: It has no credit risk, because the issuer guarantees the principal.
options.C: Its payments link to an index, and it repays at least the amount paid for it.
options.D: It can be sold before maturity for the full amount paid, at any time.

questions.rationale: Under the Bank Act, a PPN pays amounts linked to an index or reference point and repays at least the amount paid. It may pay no interest. It still carries the issuer's credit risk, and it can be hard to sell before maturity.
questions.source_quote: "provides that the principal amount that the institution is obligated to repay at or before the note’s maturity is equal to or greater than the total paid by the person for the note." — research/sources/gov/bank-act-ppn-disclosure-extracts.txt Bank Act s.627.01 'principal-protected note', ~L41

questions.stem: Which feature defines an alternative mutual fund (a "liquid alt")?

options.A: Its objectives let it borrow, sell short or use derivatives beyond conventional fund limits.
options.B: It sells its units only to accredited investors under a prospectus exemption.
options.C: Its units trade only on an exchange, and investors have no right to redeem them.
options.D: It invests only in private companies, through a limited partnership structure.

questions.rationale: An alternative mutual fund is a public mutual fund with a prospectus. Its objectives permit commodities, crypto assets, specified derivatives, borrowing or short selling in a manner not permitted for other mutual funds. Hedge funds, not liquid alts, use prospectus exemptions.
questions.source_quote: "that has adopted fundamental investment objectives that permit it to invest in physical commodities, crypto assets or specified derivatives, to borrow cash or engage in short selling in a manner not permitted for other mutual funds under this Instrument;" — research/sources/csa/ni-81-102-investment-funds.txt NI 81-102 s.1.1 'alternative mutual fund', ~L220

questions.stem: A hedge fund charges a 20% performance fee above an 8% hurdle rate and uses a high-water mark. This year its NAVPS starts above its previous peak and rises 6%. Does the manager earn a performance fee?

options.A: Yes, because the NAVPS is above its high-water mark for the year.
options.B: Yes, on the full 6% return, because the fund had no losses this year.
options.C: No, because a performance fee applies only in the year after a loss.
options.D: No, because the return for the year is below the 8% hurdle rate.

questions.rationale: A hurdle rate is the minimum return before the manager earns any performance fee. The fund is above its high-water mark, so that test passes. But the 6% return is below the 8% hurdle, so the manager earns no performance fee.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 5.14 fees: management, performance, hurdle rate, high-water mark

questions.stem: Jonah had net income before taxes of $180,000 in each of the last 2 calendar years. His spouse had $140,000 in each year, and they expect similar income this year. Does Jonah meet an accredited investor income test?

options.A: No, because his own net income is below $200,000.
options.B: No, because his financial assets are not shown to exceed $1 million.
options.C: Yes, because their combined net income is more than $300,000.
options.D: Yes, because his own net income is more than $150,000.

questions.rationale: Form 45-106F9 has a combined test with a spouse. Combined net income must exceed $300,000 in each of the 2 most recent years, and be expected this year. Their total is $320,000. He fails the $200,000 individual test, but one test is enough.
questions.source_quote: "Your net income before taxes combined with your spouse’s was more than $300,000 in each of the 2 most recent calendar years" — research/sources/csa/form-45-106f9-individual-accredited-investor-risk-acknowledgement.txt Form 45-106F9 s.3, ~L55

questions.stem: An investor buys units of a listed trust. The trust holds an operating business and pays out most of its cash flow. Which product is this?

options.A: An income trust
options.B: A real estate investment trust
options.C: A closed-end bond fund
options.D: A mutual fund trust

questions.rationale: An income trust is a listed trust that holds an operating business and pays out most of its cash flow. A REIT is the closest distractor, but a REIT owns income-producing real estate, not an operating business. The income trust payout is not guaranteed.

questions.stem: A closed-end fund lets investors redeem units once a year, on a date set in its prospectus. Which limit applies to the redemption price?

options.A: It must equal the closing market price on the exchange.
options.B: It must not be more than the net asset value of the unit.
options.C: It must not be less than the net asset value of the unit.
options.D: It must equal the issue price of the unit at the IPO.

questions.rationale: NI 81-102 says the redemption price of a non-redeemable investment fund must not be more than NAV. So the fund may pay NAV or less. A minimum of NAV is wrong, because many such funds pay NAV only once a year and a lower price at other times.
questions.source_quote: "The redemption price of a security of a non-redeemable investment fund must not be a price that is more than the net asset value of the security determined on a redemption date specified in the prospectus of the investment fund." — research/sources/csa/ni-81-102-investment-funds.txt NI 81-102 s.10.3(4), ~L2649

questions.stem: An investment fund wants to buy a controlling stake in a private manufacturer so that it can direct the company's management. How does this purpose relate to the NI 81-106 definition of a non-redeemable investment fund?

options.A: The definition allows control, because the fund need not redeem units on demand.
options.B: The definition allows control only up to 20% of the fund's net asset value.
options.C: The definition excludes a fund that invests to control an issuer, other than another investment fund.
options.D: The definition allows control if the fund's units trade on an exchange.

questions.rationale: By definition, a non-redeemable investment fund does not invest to control an issuer or to take an active part in its management. The exception is an investment in another investment fund. The 20% figure is a distractor from the single-issuer and illiquid-asset limits, not the definition.
questions.source_quote: "that does not invest, (i) for the purpose of exercising or seeking to exercise control of an issuer, other than an issuer that is a mutual fund or a non-redeemable investment fund, or (ii) for the purpose of being actively involved in the management of any issuer in which it invests" — research/sources/csa/ni-81-106-investment-fund-continuous-disclosure-nav-mer.txt NI 81-106 s.1.1 'non-redeemable investment fund' (b), ~L278-284

questions.stem: A fund of funds invests in units of an underlying fund. Under NI 81-102 s. 2.5, which fee would break the rules?

options.A: A fee the underlying fund pays for its own audit and its own legal work
options.B: A management fee that the underlying fund includes in its own MER
options.C: An operating expense that the top fund pays for its own custody
options.D: A management fee that duplicates a fee the underlying fund pays for the same service

questions.rationale: The top fund must not pay a management or incentive fee that duplicates a fee of the underlying fund for the same service. The test is the view of a reasonable person. The underlying fund's own management fee inside its MER is normal. Only the duplicate fee at the top fund breaks the rule.
questions.source_quote: "no management fees or incentive fees are payable by the investment fund that, to a reasonable person, would duplicate a fee payable by the other investment fund for the same service," — research/sources/csa/ni-81-102-investment-funds.txt NI 81-102 s.2.5(2)(d), ~L1299

questions.stem: Which statement about a pooled fund is correct?

options.A: It has no public prospectus, and dealers sell it under exemptions, such as to accredited investors.
options.B: It files a prospectus, and the dealer must deliver Fund Facts before each purchase.
options.C: It trades on an exchange, and authorized dealers create and redeem its units.
options.D: It files a prospectus, and only registered accounts such as RRSPs may hold it.

questions.rationale: A pooled fund has no public prospectus. Dealers sell it under prospectus exemptions, for example to accredited investors, or managers use it inside discretionary programs. Fund Facts delivery applies to prospectus-qualified mutual funds, so the Fund Facts option is wrong.
questions.source_quote: "The prospectus requirement does not apply to a distribution of a security if the purchaser purchases the security as principal and is an accredited investor." — research/sources/csa/ni-45-106-prospectus-exemptions.txt NI 45-106 s.2.3(1), ~L1217

questions.stem: Under NI 41-101, which description of an ETF is correct?

options.A: A non-redeemable investment fund whose units are listed and trade on an exchange
options.B: A mutual fund in continuous distribution whose units are listed and trade on an exchange
options.C: A pooled fund that sells its units only to accredited investors on an exchange
options.D: A mutual fund that issues units only once, at its initial public offering

questions.rationale: In law, an ETF is a mutual fund in continuous distribution whose securities are listed and trade on an exchange. A listed non-redeemable investment fund is a closed-end fund, not an ETF. A closed-end fund issues units mainly at its IPO.
questions.source_quote: "“ETF” or “exchange-traded mutual fund” means a mutual fund in continuous distribution, the securities of which are (a) listed on an exchange, and (b) trading on an exchange or an alternative trading system;" — research/sources/csa/ni-41-101-general-prospectus-requirements.txt NI 41-101 s.1.1 'ETF', ~L342

questions.stem: An alternative mutual fund holds 14% of its NAV in the shares of one corporation. A new purchase would take the position to 18% of NAV. Is the purchase permitted?

options.A: No, because the single-issuer limit for every mutual fund is 10% of NAV.
options.B: No, because an alternative mutual fund must keep each issuer below 15% of NAV.
options.C: Yes, because the single-issuer limit for an alternative mutual fund is 20% of NAV.
options.D: Yes, because an alternative mutual fund has no single-issuer limit at all.

questions.rationale: The 10% single-issuer limit applies to a conventional mutual fund. For an alternative mutual fund or a non-redeemable investment fund, the limit is 20% of NAV. An 18% position is below that limit, so the purchase is permitted.
questions.source_quote: "immediately after the transaction, more than 20% of its net asset value would be invested in securities of any one issuer." — research/sources/csa/ni-81-102-investment-funds.txt NI 81-102 s.2.1(1.1), ~L1037

questions.stem: A conventional mutual fund buys an index participation unit (IPU). How does the fund treat the IPU for the 10% single-issuer limit?

options.A: The purchase is exempt, and the fund ignores the securities that the IPU holds.
options.B: The fund counts the IPU as one issuer, so it can hold at most 10% of NAV in it.
options.C: The fund counts the full value of each security in the index as its own holding.
options.D: The purchase is exempt, but the fund counts its proportionate share of the securities the IPU holds.

questions.rationale: The limit does not apply to the purchase of an IPU of an investment fund. But the fund looks through the IPU. It is considered to hold directly its proportionate share of the securities that the IPU issuer holds. So the IPU is not simply ignored.
questions.source_quote: "the investment fund is considered to hold directly the underlying interest of that specified derivative or its proportionate share of the securities held by the issuer of the index participation unit." — research/sources/csa/ni-81-102-investment-funds.txt NI 81-102 s.2.1(3), ~L1063

questions.stem: A conventional mutual fund holds 9.5% of its NAV directly in shares of Northgate Mining. It also holds an IPU. Northgate Mining is 6% of the IPU's holdings. Does the IPU add to the fund's Northgate position for the 10% limit?

options.A: No, because a security that is less than 10% of the IPU's holdings is considered not held.
options.B: Yes, because the fund must always add its proportionate share of each IPU holding.
options.C: No, because the fund never looks through an IPU for the single-issuer limit.
options.D: Yes, because a direct holding above 9% makes every indirect holding count.

questions.rationale: The fund looks through an IPU to its proportionate share of the holdings. But a security that is less than 10% of the IPU's holdings is considered not held. Northgate is 6%, so it does not count. The no-look-through option is wrong, because look-through is the normal rule.
questions.source_quote: "an investment fund is considered to not hold a security or instrument if that security or instrument is a component of, but represents less than 10% of," — research/sources/csa/ni-81-102-investment-funds.txt NI 81-102 s.2.1(4), ~L1069

questions.stem: A conventional mutual fund wants to raise one position above 10% of its NAV. For which kind of security does the single-issuer limit not apply?

options.A: Common shares of a large Canadian bank listed on the TSX
options.B: Units of another investment fund, bought in line with s. 2.5
options.C: Bonds of a corporation that holds an AAA credit rating
options.D: Shares of a company that is part of a major stock index

questions.rationale: The single-issuer limit does not apply to five listed kinds of purchase. One is a security of another investment fund, if the purchase meets s. 2.5. A high credit rating or index membership gives no exemption. A bank's common shares are also subject to the limit.
questions.source_quote: "a security issued by an investment fund if the purchase is made in accordance with the requirements of section 2.5;" — research/sources/csa/ni-81-102-investment-funds.txt NI 81-102 s.2.1(2)(c), ~L1054

questions.stem: Vesna wants a fund that excludes fossil-fuel producers. Two funds that she likes both use the word "sustainable" in their names. What should her RR do first?

options.A: Recommend either fund, because the label means that both exclude fossil fuels.
options.B: Recommend the fund with the lower MER, because the two mandates are the same.
options.C: Compare each fund's objectives and holdings, because ESG mandates differ.
options.D: Recommend the fund with the higher risk rating, because ESG funds lag.

questions.rationale: ESG mandates can screen out industries, integrate ESG factors into analysis, or target an impact. Labels vary. So the RR must read each fund's objectives and holdings to find out if it excludes fossil-fuel producers. A name alone does not prove an exclusion screen.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 5.2 (ESG labels vary; read objectives and holdings)

questions.stem: Zoltan has $5,000. He wants exposure to emerging-market government bonds, which are hard for him to buy directly. Which advantage of a managed product is most relevant to him?

options.A: Control over each holding and the timing of each gain
options.B: Protection from all losses through a guarantee of principal
options.C: Freedom from all ongoing fees that reduce annual returns
options.D: Access to markets that are hard for a small investor to reach

questions.rationale: A fund gives access to hard-to-reach markets, with diversification and professional management for a small sum. A fund does not give control over holdings or gains. Ongoing fees (the MER) reduce returns every year. Most funds have no guarantee.

questions.stem: Two funds have the same mandate and similar holdings. One fund has an MER that is 1.2 percentage points higher. Under IDPC 3402(1), which factor must the dealer consider before it recommends that fund?

options.A: The potential and actual impact of costs on the client's returns
options.B: Only the risk rating, because the two mandates are the same
options.C: Only the amount of the minimum investment for each fund
options.D: The revenue that the dealer earns from each of the funds

questions.rationale: IDPC 3402(1) makes the dealer consider the potential and actual impact of costs on the retail client's returns. A higher MER reduces the client's return every year. The same risk rating does not remove the cost factor. Dealer revenue is not a suitability factor.
questions.source_quote: "the potential and actual impact of costs on the retail client’s returns, and" — research/sources/ciro/idpc-rules-2026-08-11.txt IDPC 3402(1)(i)(d), ~L6806

questions.stem: Which product may a mutual fund dealer sell to its clients?

options.A: Common shares of a company listed on the TSX
options.B: Shares of a labour-sponsored investment fund corporation
options.C: Bonds that a large Canadian corporation issues
options.D: Options on the shares of a listed company

questions.rationale: An investment dealer may deal in any security. A mutual fund dealer may deal only in mutual funds and certain other investment funds, such as labour-sponsored funds. Listed shares, corporate bonds and options are outside its category.
questions.source_quote: "an investment fund that is a labour-sponsored investment fund corporation or labour-sponsored venture capital corporation" — research/sources/csa/ni-31-103-parts-2-7-8-11-categories-exemptions-records.txt NI 31-103 s.7.1(2)(b)(ii), ~L224

questions.stem: In a mutual fund trust, which participant holds legal title to the portfolio assets for the investors?

options.A: The custodian
options.B: The manager
options.C: The trustee
options.D: The principal distributor

questions.rationale: In a trust, the trustee holds legal title to the assets for the investors. The custodian is the closest distractor, but it has physical custody of the assets, not legal title. The manager directs the fund's business.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 5.3 (trustee holds legal title; custodian physical custody)

questions.stem: A mutual fund needs a custodian for its assets in Canada. Which institution qualifies under NI 81-102?

options.A: A licensed trust company with equity of $6,000,000
options.B: The fund's own manager, if it holds enough capital
options.C: Any firm that the manager selects, if it discloses this
options.D: A licensed trust company with equity of $25,000,000

questions.rationale: For assets in Canada, the custodian must be a qualified institution. Examples are a Schedule I, II or III bank and a trust company with equity of not less than $10,000,000. A $6,000,000 trust company is too small. The manager must not act as custodian.
questions.source_quote: "a trust company that is incorporated under the laws of Canada or a jurisdiction and licensed or registered under the laws of Canada or a jurisdiction, and that has equity, as reported in its most recent audited financial statements, of not less than $10,000,000;" — research/sources/csa/ni-81-102-part-6-custodianship-part-11-commingling-of-cash.txt NI 81-102 s.6.2(2), ~L93

questions.stem: According to Fund Facts, what is the trailing commission for?

options.A: The services and advice that the representative and the firm give to the investor
options.B: The trading costs that the fund pays when it buys and sells its securities
options.C: A one-time payment to the dealer when the investor first buys the fund
options.D: The fees that the custodian charges to hold the assets of the fund

questions.rationale: Fund Facts says the trailing commission is for the services and advice that the representative and their firm provide. It is paid for as long as the investor owns the fund, out of the management fee. It is not a one-time payment.
questions.source_quote: "It is for the services and advice that your representative and their firm provide to you." — research/sources/csa/form-81-101f3-fund-facts.txt Form 81-101F3 Part II Item 1.3(6), ~L849

questions.stem: Silas wants to redeem his mutual fund units. A friend tells him the manager will charge him a deferred sales charge (DSC). Which statement is correct under NI 81-102?

options.A: The manager may charge a DSC if he redeems within seven years of purchase.
options.B: The manager must not charge him a fee for the redemption, so no DSC applies.
options.C: The manager may charge a DSC if the Fund Facts discloses the schedule.
options.D: The manager may charge a DSC, but only if he redeems after the cut-off time.

questions.rationale: NI 81-102 says a manager must not charge a securityholder a fee for a redemption. So a manager cannot charge a DSC. Disclosure in Fund Facts does not make a prohibited fee permitted. Short-term trading fees are a separate matter.
questions.source_quote: "A manager must not charge a fee to a securityholder of a mutual fund for a redemption by the securityholder of securities of the mutual fund." — research/sources/csa/ni-81-102-investment-funds.txt NI 81-102 s.10.2.1, ~L2631

questions.stem: Keziah holds Series A shares of one class of a mutual fund corporation. She switches to Series F of the same class. The two series differ only in fees. What is the tax effect?

options.A: The switch is a disposition, so she must report any capital gain.
options.B: The switch is a disposition, but only if the series NAVPS differ.
options.C: The switch is not a disposition, so it does not trigger a capital gain.
options.D: The switch is not a disposition, but she must restart her ACB at zero.

questions.rationale: If only the fees or expenses differ, a switch between series of the same class is not a disposition. A switch between different classes of a mutual fund corporation can be a taxable disposition. Her switch stays within one class.
questions.source_quote: "where the only difference is the relative management fees or expenses paid by the investor in the classes of shares (switch is between different series of the same class of shares), there is no disposition." — research/sources/cra/guide-t4037-capital-gains-2025.txt CRA T4037 (2025) 'Mutual funds' tax tip, ~L1635

questions.stem: An investment fund does not use specified derivatives or sell short. It calculated its NAV monthly when NI 81-106 came into force, and it still does. What is its minimum NAV frequency?

options.A: Weekly, because no fund may calculate NAV less often than weekly
options.B: Every business day, because all mutual funds must price daily
options.C: Quarterly, because it uses no specified derivatives or short sales
options.D: Monthly, because the transition exception lets it keep that frequency

questions.rationale: The normal minimum for such a fund is weekly. But a fund that calculated NAV at least monthly when NI 81-106 came into force may keep that frequency. This exception applies only to the weekly minimum. Daily pricing is industry practice, not a universal rule.
questions.source_quote: "an investment fund that, at the date that this Instrument comes into force, calculates net asset value no less frequently than once a month may continue to calculate net asset value at least as frequently as it does at that date." — research/sources/csa/ni-81-106-investment-fund-continuous-disclosure-nav-mer.txt NI 81-106 s.14.2(5), ~L447

questions.stem: Which statement describes a fee-based series of a mutual fund?

options.A: It pays no trailing commission, and investors hold it in a fee-based account.
options.B: It pays a higher trailing commission, and investors hold it in any account.
options.C: It charges a deferred sales charge, and investors hold it in a fee-based account.
options.D: It pays no management fee, and investors hold it only in a registered account.

questions.rationale: A fee-based series pays no trailing commission. To buy it, the investor must take part in a fee-based arrangement with the dealer. The series still pays a management fee, so the no-management-fee option is wrong.
questions.source_quote: "requirement for an investor to participate in a fee-based arrangement with their dealer in order to be eligible to purchase the particular class or series" — research/sources/csa/form-81-101f3-fund-facts.txt Form 81-101F3 Part II Item 1.4 Instruction (1), ~L933

questions.stem: Which cost forms part of a mutual fund's management expense ratio (MER)?

options.A: The front-end sales charge that the investor pays
options.B: The trailing commission paid out of the management fee
options.C: The switch fee that the investor pays to the dealer
options.D: The short-term trading fee that the investor pays

questions.rationale: The MER is the total of the management fee, including the trailing commission, and the operating expenses. The fund pays these costs. A front-end sales charge, a switch fee and a short-term trading fee are paid by the investor directly, so they are not in the MER.
questions.source_quote: "This is the total of the fund’s management fee (including the trailing commission) and operating expenses." — research/sources/csa/form-81-101f3-fund-facts.txt Form 81-101F3 Part II Item 1.3(2), ~L782

questions.stem: Under NI 81-102 Appendix F, which data does a mutual fund use to set its investment risk level?

options.A: Annual returns over the most recent 5 years, with distributions paid in cash
options.B: The largest decline in NAV over the life of the fund, with no reinvestment
options.C: Monthly returns over the most recent 10 years, with distributions reinvested
options.D: The fund's beta against its benchmark over the most recent 3 years

questions.rationale: Appendix F uses one mandatory method. The fund takes its monthly returns over the most recent 10 years, calculated from NAV with all distributions reinvested. It then finds the annualized standard deviation and places it in one of five bands.
questions.source_quote: "A mutual fund must calculate its standard deviation for the most recent 10 years as follows:" — research/sources/csa/ni-81-102-investment-funds.txt NI 81-102 Appendix F Item 2(1), ~L3725

questions.stem: A fund's standard deviation places it in the "Low to medium" band. The manager believes this understates the fund's risk. What may the manager do?

options.A: Nothing, because the band from the calculation is final and cannot change
options.B: Lower the risk level if that is reasonable, and tell investors in a notice
options.C: Replace the fund's own returns with a reference index that has more volatility
options.D: Raise the risk level if that is reasonable, and keep records of how it set the level

questions.rationale: Under Appendix F, the manager may increase the investment risk level if that is reasonable in the circumstances. The manager must keep records of how it set the level. The rule permits an increase, not a decrease, so the lower-level option is wrong.
questions.source_quote: "the investment risk level of a mutual fund may be increased if doing so is reasonable in the circumstances." — research/sources/csa/ni-81-102-investment-funds.txt NI 81-102 Appendix F Item 1(2), ~L3688

questions.stem: A U.S. equity fund offers an unhedged series and a currency-hedged series. The hedging results in a different risk level for the hedged series. How does the hedged series set its risk level?

options.A: It uses its own returns to calculate its own risk level.
options.B: It uses the risk level that the unhedged series calculated.
options.C: It uses the higher of the two levels for both series.
options.D: It uses a reference index chosen for the hedged series.

questions.rationale: If a series has an attribute that results in a different risk level, the series uses its own returns. Currency hedging is an example of such an attribute. A reference index applies only to missing history when no qualifying proxy fund exists.
questions.source_quote: "if a series or class of securities of the mutual fund has an attribute that results in a different investment risk level for the series or class than the investment risk level of the mutual fund, the return on investment for that series or class of securities must be used" — research/sources/csa/ni-81-102-investment-funds.txt NI 81-102 Appendix F Item 3, ~L3760

questions.stem: A new fund has 3 years of returns. No underlying fund exists. Another fund has 12 years of history and the same manager, objectives and strategies, but a different portfolio manager. Which returns fill the missing 7 years?

options.A: The returns of the other fund, because it has the same manager and objectives
options.B: The returns of a reference index that reasonably approximates the fund's standard deviation
options.C: The returns of the other fund, but only for the most recent 7 of its 12 years
options.D: No returns, because the fund uses only its own 3 years until it has 10

questions.rationale: The matching-fund proxy needs the same manager, portfolio manager, objectives and strategies. A different portfolio manager means it does not qualify. With no clone or matching fund, the fund must use a reference index for the missing years. It cannot use only its own 3 years.
questions.source_quote: "the mutual fund must select a reference index in accordance with Item 5" — research/sources/csa/ni-81-102-investment-funds.txt NI 81-102 Appendix F Item 4(2), ~L3790

questions.stem: A fund uses a reference index to fill in missing years of its risk calculation. Which further duty applies to the manager?

options.A: Replace the index each year with the fund's own most recent returns
options.B: Get unitholder approval for the index before the fund can use it
options.C: Monitor the index at least annually and describe it in the prospectus
options.D: Show the index returns as the fund's own returns in its Fund Facts

questions.rationale: If a fund uses a reference index, it must monitor the reasonableness of the index at least annually. It must also give a brief description of the index in its prospectus. The rule needs no unitholder vote.
questions.source_quote: "monitor the reasonableness of the reference index on an annual basis or more frequently if necessary," — research/sources/csa/ni-81-102-investment-funds.txt NI 81-102 Appendix F Item 5(2)(a), ~L3832

questions.stem: Thaddeus holds an unhedged U.S. equity fund. This year U.S. stock prices are flat, and the Canadian dollar rises against the U.S. dollar. What happens to his holding in Canadian-dollar terms?

options.A: Its value rises, because a stronger Canadian dollar buys more U.S. shares.
options.B: Its value stays the same, because U.S. stock prices did not change.
options.C: Its value stays the same, because funds hedge currency risk by law.
options.D: Its value falls, because the U.S. holdings are worth fewer Canadian dollars.

questions.rationale: Currency is a source of risk for foreign funds. If the Canadian dollar rises, unhedged foreign holdings fall in Canadian-dollar value. Flat U.S. prices do not offset the currency loss. No rule makes funds hedge currency risk.

questions.stem: Which item is a disadvantage of a mutual fund to its provider, the fund manager?

options.A: Redemptions can force asset sales, and disclosure costs are high.
options.B: The fund earns asset-based fee income for the manager each year.
options.C: Recurring contributions add to the assets that the manager runs.
options.D: Scale lets the manager spread its fixed costs over more assets.

questions.rationale: For the provider, the disadvantages are redemptions that force asset sales, disclosure and compliance costs, and fee pressure from ETFs. Asset-based fee income, recurring contributions and scale are advantages to the provider.

questions.stem: Tamsin's mutual fund pays her a return of capital distribution. Which statement about this distribution is correct?

options.A: It is interest that the fund earned on its bond holdings this year.
options.B: It pays back part of her own money, not a return on her investment.
options.C: It is a capital gain that the fund realized on its portfolio sales.
options.D: It is a dividend that the fund received from Canadian corporations.

questions.rationale: Return comes from income distributions, capital gains distributions and NAV growth. A return of capital is different. It is the investor's own money paid back, not a return on it. Interest, capital gains and dividends are returns on the investment.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 5.4 (sources of return; return of capital)

questions.stem: During a market sell-off, many investors redeem units of a bond mutual fund at the same time. The manager must sell bonds at poor prices. Who bears the cost of these sales?

options.A: The manager pays it out of its own management fee.
options.B: The redeeming investors pay it through a redemption fee to the manager.
options.C: The investors who remain in the fund share that cost.
options.D: The custodian pays it, because it holds the fund's assets.

questions.rationale: If many investors redeem at once, the manager must sell assets, perhaps at poor prices. The remaining investors share that cost. A manager must not charge a fee for a redemption, so the redemption-fee option is wrong.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 5.4 (redemptions force asset sales; remaining investors bear cost)

questions.stem: According to Fund Facts, what is typically true of a fund with higher volatility?

options.A: It has a smaller chance of losing money and a greater chance of higher returns.
options.B: It has a greater chance of losing money and no chance of higher returns.
options.C: It has the same chance of losing money as a fund with lower volatility.
options.D: It has a greater chance of losing money and may have a greater chance of higher returns.

questions.rationale: Fund Facts says that funds with higher volatility typically have a greater chance of losing money. They may also have a greater chance of higher returns. Volatility works in both directions, so a one-sided option is wrong.
questions.source_quote: "In general, funds with higher volatility will have returns that change more over time. They typically have a greater chance of losing money and may have a greater chance of higher returns." — research/sources/csa/form-81-101f3-fund-facts.txt Form 81-101F3 Part I Item 4(1), ~L379

questions.stem: Esme buys ETF units through her dealer, which acts as her agent. The dealer has not given her the ETF Facts before. When must it deliver the ETF Facts?

options.A: Not later than midnight on the second business day after the purchase
options.B: Before it accepts her instruction to buy the ETF units
options.C: Within 10 days after the purchase, with her account statement
options.D: Only if she asks for the document after the purchase
