options.D: A multi-factor loading

questions.rationale: Maximum drawdown is the largest decline from a previous peak to a later trough in a period. Variance measures how widely returns scatter around their mean. Beta measures sensitivity to the market.

questions.stem: Two bond-heavy balanced funds have the same market beta. When interest rates rise, one fund falls much more than the other. Which measure shows this difference?

options.A: The market beta of each fund
options.B: Separate loadings on each risk factor
options.C: The ratio of each fund's beta to the market
options.D: The weighted-average beta of the two funds

questions.rationale: Multi-factor measures give a separate loading, like a beta, for each risk source, such as interest rates. Two funds with the same market beta can react very differently to rates. A single beta hides that difference.

questions.stem: Rosalind Achebe holds a Canadian equity fund. She can add one of four assets with the same expected return and standard deviation. Which correlation with her fund lowers her portfolio risk most?
questions.rationale: The lower the correlation, the larger the reduction in portfolio standard deviation. A correlation of −0.3 is the lowest of the four. A correlation near +1 gives almost no risk reduction.

questions.stem: Ewan Szabo has a large position in one stock with a large unrealized capital gain. He fears a sharp fall in the next three months. He does not want to sell this year. Which action best fits?

options.A: Sell the shares and buy a broad index fund
options.B: Buy more shares if the price falls
options.C: Buy put options on the shares he holds
options.D: Sell short shares of an unrelated company

questions.rationale: A protective put sets a minimum value for his shares and keeps his upside, less the premium. It suits a temporary concern when he has a tax reason not to sell. A sale and index purchase would diversify, but it realizes the capital gain.

questions.stem: Matthias Ferreira sells a stock short in his margin account. The price of the stock then rises a lot. What happens to the credit balance that his account must hold?

options.A: It decreases, because the short-sale proceeds grow with the price of the stock
options.B: It stays fixed, because the requirement is set on the day of the short sale
options.C: It increases, because the requirement is a percentage of the current market value
options.D: It falls to zero, because the dealer has already borrowed the shares to deliver

questions.rationale: A short position has a negative loan value equal to (100% + margin rate) times its market value. The account must hold a credit at least equal to that value (IDPC 5113). So the required credit rises with the price.
questions.source_quote: "the cash balance in the margin account must be a credit equal to or larger than the net negative loan value for the account to be in good standing" — research/sources/ciro/idpc-rules-2026-08-11.txt IDPC 5113(4)(iii), ~line 14796

questions.stem: Priyanka Holloway bought 500 shares yesterday. The trade has not settled, so she has not received the shares. Today she sells them. How does UMIR treat this sale?

options.A: It is a short sale, because she has not yet received the shares
options.B: It is not a short sale, because she is deemed to own the shares
options.C: It is a short sale, unless the dealer borrows the shares first
options.D: It is not a short sale, but only if she holds a margin account

questions.rationale: Under the UMIR definition, a seller who purchased a security but has not yet received delivery is deemed to own it. So the sale is not a short sale. Borrowed shares, by contrast, do not count as owned.
questions.source_quote: "has purchased or has entered into an unconditional contract to purchase the security, but has not yet received delivery of the security" — research/sources/ciro/umir-2026-08-11.txt UMIR 1.1 "short sale" (a), ~line 2467

questions.stem: Which risk applies to a client who sells a stock short but not to a client who buys the same stock?

options.A: The loss can equal the full amount invested
options.B: The client receives dividends from the issuer
options.C: The value falls if the issuer cuts its profits
options.D: The loss has no upper limit if the price rises

questions.rationale: A short seller loses as the price rises, and the price can rise without limit. A buyer can lose at most the amount invested. A short seller pays dividends on borrowed shares and does not receive them.

questions.stem: What is the starting point of the Black–Litterman model before the manager adds any views?

options.A: The market's equilibrium returns implied by market-capitalization weights
options.B: The historical average return of each asset in the portfolio
options.C: An equal weight in each asset, with no regard to correlations
options.D: A distribution of outcomes from thousands of random return paths

questions.rationale: Black–Litterman starts from market equilibrium (implied) returns from market-capitalization weights. It then blends in the manager's views, weighted by confidence. It does not start from historical averages. Random return paths describe Monte Carlo simulation.

questions.stem: Leontyne Park holds 12 stocks in equal amounts. All 12 companies are Canadian oil and gas producers. Which statement describes her portfolio?

options.A: Efficient diversification near the frontier
options.B: Naive diversification with industry concentration
options.C: Issuer concentration in one company
options.D: An allocation from the Black–Litterman model

questions.rationale: She spreads money equally across many holdings with no regard to correlations, which is naive diversification. All 12 companies react to the same news, so she has industry concentration. Issuer concentration means one oversized holding.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.6 naive diversification and concentration

questions.stem: Which asset pricing model adds a momentum factor to the three Fama–French factors of market, size and value?

options.A: The Fama–French five-factor model
options.B: The arbitrage pricing theory
options.C: The Carhart four-factor model
options.D: The capital asset pricing model

questions.rationale: The Carhart model is the three Fama–French factors plus momentum. The Fama–French five-factor model adds profitability and investment, not momentum. The CAPM uses only the market factor.

questions.stem: A small-cap value fund has a positive CAPM alpha. With a Fama–French model, its alpha is close to zero. What does this difference most likely show?

options.A: Its extra return came mostly from size and value factor exposure
options.B: Its manager has stock-selection skill that the Fama–French model hides
options.C: Its beta to the market is negative, so the CAPM understates its return
options.D: Its returns came from momentum, which the Fama–French model ignores

questions.rationale: The CAPM counts only market risk, so it labels extra return from small-cap and value stocks as alpha. The Fama–French model counts size and value as factors, and little extra return remains. So the result came from factor exposure, not skill.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.7 scenario (CAPM vs Fama-French alpha)

questions.stem: The risk-free rate is 2.5% and the expected market return is 9%. A stock has a beta of 1.4. What is its expected return under the CAPM?
questions.rationale: The market risk premium is 9% − 2.5% = 6.5%. Expected return = 2.5% + 1.4 × 6.5% = 11.6%. The 12.6% result multiplies beta by the market return, not by the premium. The 9.1% result omits the risk-free rate.

questions.stem: A portfolio holds 40% in a stock with a beta of 1.5, 35% in a stock with a beta of 0.9 and 25% in T-bills. The risk-free rate is 3% and the expected market return is 8%. What is the portfolio's CAPM expected return?
questions.rationale: Portfolio beta = 0.40(1.5) + 0.35(0.9) + 0.25(0) = 0.915. Expected return = 3% + 0.915 × 5% = 7.58%. The 7.00% result uses a simple average of the three betas. T-bills have a beta of zero but still count in the weights.

questions.stem: The risk-free rate is 4% and the expected market return is 10%. A stock has a beta of 0.8. An analyst forecasts an 8.0% return for it. Which conclusion is correct?

options.A: Required return is 8.8%; the stock plots above the SML and is undervalued
options.B: Required return is 8.8%; the stock plots below the SML and is overvalued
options.C: Required return is 8.0%; the stock plots on the SML and is fairly priced
options.D: Required return is 12.0%; the stock plots below the SML and is overvalued

questions.rationale: Required return = 4% + 0.8 × (10% − 4%) = 8.8%. The 8.0% forecast is below the required return, so the stock plots below the SML and is overvalued. The 8.0% figure multiplies beta by the market return.

questions.stem: Suppose the market is semi-strong efficient but not strong-form efficient. Which approach can still give consistent abnormal returns?

options.A: Trading on material private information
options.B: Technical analysis of past prices
options.C: Fundamental analysis of public reports
options.D: Purchases of recent top performers

questions.rationale: Semi-strong efficiency means prices reflect all public information, so technical and fundamental analysis of public data fail. Only private information can still give an edge. The strong form rules out even that.

questions.stem: Suppose the market is weak-form efficient but not semi-strong efficient. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Technical analysis of price patterns can still give abnormal returns
options.B: No approach can give abnormal returns, not even private information
options.C: Only a passive index fund can match the return of the market
options.D: Fundamental analysis of public data can still give abnormal returns

questions.rationale: Weak-form efficiency means prices reflect past price and volume data, so technical analysis fails. It does not rule out abnormal returns from fundamental analysis. Only the semi-strong form rules those out.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.9 exam trap (weak vs semi-strong)

questions.stem: Caspian Moreau buys any stock with a low price-to-book ratio and a high dividend yield. He pays no attention to the sector or the economy. Which technique does he use?

options.A: Top-down sector rotation
options.B: Bottom-up growth investing
options.C: Market timing
options.D: Bottom-up value investing

questions.rationale: Company ratios such as low price-to-book and high dividend yield drive his choices, so he is a bottom-up value manager. A sector rotator starts from a forecast of the business cycle and overweights sectors.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.10 value investing and exam trap

questions.stem: Ines Kowalczyk cuts her fund's equity weight from 85% to 30% because she expects a recession. She plans to buy equities again at the recovery. Which risk is most specific to her technique?

options.A: She can buy a cheap stock whose business is in permanent decline
options.B: She must be right about both the exit and the return to equities
options.C: Her stocks can lose both earnings and P/E multiple if growth slows
options.D: Her fund's return can differ from the index because of sampling

questions.rationale: This is market timing: a large switch out of equities on a forecast. A timer must be right twice, and out of the market can miss a few very strong days. A value trap is the main risk of value investing.

questions.stem: Radomir Ellison holds only a growth fund. Its stocks trade at high P/E multiples. Economists now forecast slower earnings growth. Why can the fund's price fall sharply?

options.A: The stocks can become value traps with low P/E
options.B: The fund holds too much in defensive sectors
options.C: Both the earnings and the P/E multiple can fall
options.D: The fund's dividends must rise to keep investors

questions.rationale: Growth stock prices already include the expected growth. If growth slows, earnings fall and investors pay a lower P/E multiple, so the price drops from two sources. A value trap is a cheap, low-P/E stock in permanent decline.

questions.stem: Two ETFs track the same index. ETF P has a tracking difference of −0.15% and a tracking error of 0.40%. ETF Q has a tracking difference of −0.35% and a tracking error of 0.08%. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Q lags the index less on average, but P follows the index more consistently
options.B: P lags the index less on average, but Q follows the index more consistently
options.C: P lags the index less and also follows the index more consistently
options.D: Q lags the index less and also follows the index more consistently

questions.rationale: Tracking difference is the gap between fund and index returns, so P's smaller gap means it lags less. Tracking error is the variability of that gap, so Q's lower figure means it follows the index more consistently.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.11 tracking difference vs tracking error

questions.stem: Tobiah Lindqvist says that his S&P/TSX Composite index fund is safe because it is passive. Which reply is accurate?

options.A: The fund carries full market risk; passive management mainly removes security-selection risk
options.B: The fund carries no market risk; its only risk is tracking error against the index
options.C: The fund moves to cash when the market falls, so it protects the client from declines
options.D: The fund removes systematic risk, because it holds every stock in the index

questions.rationale: Index funds are not risk-free. They carry full market (systematic) risk and give no protection when the market falls. Passive management largely removes manager (security-selection) risk, not market risk. Diversification cannot remove systematic risk.

questions.stem: A manager must fund a fixed payment due in six years. Which step immunizes the bond portfolio against changes in interest rates?

options.A: Set the portfolio's average maturity equal to six years
options.B: Buy one six-year coupon bond and hold it to maturity
options.C: Set the portfolio's duration as short as possible
options.D: Set the portfolio's Macaulay duration equal to six years

questions.rationale: Immunization matches duration, not maturity, to the horizon. A coupon bond's duration is shorter than its maturity, so a six-year coupon bond does not immunize a six-year payment. The manager must also rebalance as duration drifts.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.12 immunization and exam trap

questions.stem: A bond manager expects credit spreads to narrow. The manager has no view on the general level of interest rates. Which active technique fits this forecast?

options.A: Move from corporate bonds toward government bonds
options.B: Lengthen the portfolio's duration
options.C: Build a ladder of staggered maturities
options.D: Move from government bonds toward corporate bonds

questions.rationale: This is bond sector rotation. When spreads narrow, corporate bonds gain relative to government bonds, so the manager moves toward corporates. Lengthening duration is a bet on falling rates, and the manager has no rate view.

questions.stem: In the usual order of portfolio construction, which step comes directly after the manager identifies the client's constraints?

options.A: Select the securities in each asset class
options.B: Monitor the portfolio and rebalance it
options.C: Choose the asset mix
options.D: Set the client's objectives

questions.rationale: The order is objectives, constraints, asset mix, security selection, then monitoring and rebalancing. Security selection comes after the mix, because the mix decides how much goes into each asset class.

questions.stem: Marisol Ekwueme manages a portfolio with a strategic mix of 60% equities. She expects strong earnings next quarter. She raises equities to 68% for that quarter only. Which type of asset allocation is this?

options.A: Strategic asset allocation
options.B: Dynamic asset allocation
options.C: Rebalancing to target weights
options.D: Tactical asset allocation

questions.rationale: A temporary, deliberate tilt from the strategic mix, based on a forecast, is tactical allocation. Dynamic allocation follows a fixed rule as market values change and needs no forecast.

questions.stem: A manager rebalances a portfolio to its fixed targets after a large market move. Which trading pattern does rebalancing cause?

options.A: The manager sells assets that rose and buys assets that fell
options.B: The manager buys more of the assets that rose most
options.C: The manager moves the targets toward the best performer
options.D: The manager holds all assets and lets the weights drift

questions.rationale: Rebalancing restores drifted weights to fixed targets. The asset that rose is now overweight, so the manager sells it and buys the asset that fell. Moving the targets changes the strategic mix.

questions.stem: Florian Abara must sell a large block of a thinly traded stock to rebalance a client portfolio. Which statement about the cost of this trade is correct?

options.A: The price can move against the client before the trade is complete
options.B: The trade has no spread cost because the block is large
options.C: The trade cannot realize a capital gain in a taxable account
options.D: The trade costs only the commission, because time has no cost

questions.rationale: Each trade costs the spread, a commission and time. In a large or illiquid trade, the price can move against the client before the trade is complete. A taxable sale can also realize a capital gain.

questions.stem: Henrike Dube's portfolio has a 60/40 target of equities and bonds. Equities rise strongly for three years. She never rebalances. What happens to her portfolio's risk?

options.A: It rises above the level that she agreed to
options.B: It stays at the level that she agreed to
options.C: It falls below the level that she agreed to
options.D: It falls, because her equity gains offset bond risk

questions.rationale: Without rebalancing, the best performer grows into a larger share. After an equity rally, the equity weight exceeds 60%, so risk drifts above the agreed level. Rebalancing keeps the agreed risk.

questions.stem: A manager wants a cheap and consistent way to choose stocks from a large list of companies. Which stock selection technique fits this goal best?

options.A: Company-by-company fundamental analysis
options.B: Detailed meetings with each company's management
options.C: A separate analyst forecast for each company
options.D: Quantitative screens

questions.rationale: Quantitative screens apply the same rules to every company at low cost. Company-by-company fundamental analysis, including management meetings and forecasts, can find mispriced stocks, but it costs more.

questions.stem: Viveka Mensah saves for a home purchase. Ten years ago, her goal was 15 years away. Now it is two years away. Under a time-horizon strategy, how does her asset mix usually change?

options.A: Her equity weight rises as the goal comes near
options.B: Her mix stays fixed until the goal date
options.C: Her cash weight falls to fund more equities
options.D: Her equity weight falls as the goal comes near

questions.rationale: A longer horizon permits more equities. As a goal comes near, the client has less time to recover from a loss, so the equity weight usually falls.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.1 (time horizon or life stage strategy)

questions.stem: Lucan Ishikawa has an advisory account. His equity weight is now outside its tolerance band. His RR wants to sell equities and buy bonds. What must the RR do first?

options.A: Make the trade, because the band breach authorizes it
options.B: Get Lucan's instruction before the trade
options.C: Make the trade and tell Lucan at the next review
options.D: Wait until the next scheduled annual rebalancing date

questions.rationale: In an advisory account, the client is responsible for all investment decisions. So the RR recommends the rebalance and gets the client's instruction first. A band breach does not give the RR discretion.
questions.source_quote: "the client is responsible for all investment decisions but is able to rely on advice given by a Registered Representative" — research/sources/ciro/idpc-rules-2026-08-11.txt IDPC 1201 'advisory account', ~line 256

questions.stem: Interest rates rise sharply. Which holding most likely has the largest fall in price?

options.A: A short-term bond with a high coupon
options.B: A 90-day Treasury bill
options.C: A long-term bond with a low coupon
options.D: A long-term bond with a high coupon

questions.rationale: Bond prices fall when rates rise. Longer terms and lower coupons make the price move more. So a long-term, high-coupon bond moves less than a long-term, low-coupon bond.

questions.stem: Saoirse Nadeau holds a five-year bond to maturity, and the issuer pays in full. At maturity, rates are much lower. She must reinvest at the lower rate. Which risk affects her?

options.A: Capital risk
options.B: Liquidity risk
options.C: Income risk
options.D: Issuer risk

questions.rationale: When a bond matures and the client must reinvest at a lower rate, her income falls. This is income (reinvestment) risk. Capital risk does not apply, because she got par back.

questions.stem: Gideon Farrow may need cash at short notice for a business deal. Most of his portfolio is in exempt-market securities that trade rarely. Which risk is most serious for him?

options.A: Inflation risk
options.B: Interest rate risk
options.C: Income risk
options.D: Liquidity risk

questions.rationale: Liquidity risk is the risk that a client cannot sell quickly at a price near fair value. Thinly traded and exempt-market securities carry it. It matters most when cash may be needed at short notice.

questions.stem: Esperanza Kowal needs her savings for a down payment in 12 months. She plans to invest them in high-yield bonds and small-cap stocks. Which risk is most serious for her?

options.A: Inflation risk
options.B: Income risk
options.C: Capital risk
options.D: Interest rate risk

questions.rationale: Capital risk is the risk that value falls below the amount invested. Equities and high-yield debt carry the most. With a 12-month horizon, she has little time to recover from a loss.

questions.stem: Which client is most exposed to income risk?

options.A: A young saver who reinvests all dividends for 30 years
options.B: A retiree who pays living costs from dividends and interest
options.C: A client who holds only growth stocks that pay no dividends
options.D: An executive who holds cash for a purchase next month

questions.rationale: Income risk is the risk that portfolio income falls, from a dividend cut or reinvestment at lower rates. Retirees who live on portfolio income are most exposed. A saver who reinvests does not depend on it.

questions.stem: Bartholomew Yeung holds most of his bond portfolio in bonds of one lower-rated company. Which step most directly reduces his issuer risk?

options.A: Buy longer-term bonds of the same company
options.B: Hold the same bonds to maturity
options.C: Buy higher-coupon bonds of the same company
options.D: Spread the bonds across many issuers

questions.rationale: Issuer risk comes from problems at one issuer, such as a default or a downgrade. Single-issuer holdings carry the most. Diversification across issuers reduces it. Holding to maturity does not prevent a default.

questions.stem: Under IDPC 3201, which situation is an example of financial exploitation of a client?

options.A: A client loses 20% of her portfolio value in a broad market decline
options.B: A client's long-term bond falls in price after interest rates rise
options.C: A relative uses undue influence to take control of an older client's savings
options.D: A client redeems a fund early and pays the fee that the fund charges

questions.rationale: IDPC 3201 defines financial exploitation as the use or control of a person's financial asset through undue influence, unlawful conduct or another wrongful act. Market losses and rate changes are investment risks.
questions.source_quote: "the use or control of, or deprivation of the use or control of, a financial asset of an individual by a person through undue influence, unlawful conduct or another wrongful act" — research/sources/ciro/idpc-rules-2026-08-11.txt IDPC 3201 definition "financial exploitation", ~line 5474

questions.stem: Which activity does CIRO's AML guidance list as a sign that may indicate money laundering?

options.A: A client rebalances her portfolio back to its target mix once a year
options.B: A client sells securities early and pays a fee, with no plausible explanation
options.C: A client buys a broad-market ETF in a registered retirement account
options.D: A client reinvests a maturing GIC in a new five-year GIC

questions.rationale: GN-3200-23-001 says that early sales that cause a fee, with no plausible explanation, could indicate money laundering. Routine rebalancing, index purchases and reinvestment have a clear investment purpose.
questions.source_quote: "If a client is selling securities early and incurring a fee without a plausible explanation, this could indicate money laundering." — research/sources/ciro/gn-3200-23-001-aml-compliance-guidance.txt GN-3200-23-001 s. 5.3.3, ~line 475

questions.stem: A new client deposits physical share certificates into a brokerage account. Why does CIRO's AML guidance treat this as a sign that needs more investigation?

options.A: Physical certificates always show that the shares are stolen
options.B: Physical certificates cannot legally be held in a margin account
options.C: There is little information that confirms the source of the funds
options.D: Physical certificates prevent the dealer from settling trades on time

questions.rationale: GN-3200-23-001 notes that certificate deposits give little information about the source of funds or how the client got them. The guidance treats this as an indicator, not as proof of a crime.
questions.source_quote: "When physical certificates are deposited into a brokerage account, there is little information confirming the source of funds or how the client obtained them." — research/sources/ciro/gn-3200-23-001-aml-compliance-guidance.txt GN-3200-23-001 s. 5.3.2, ~line 471

questions.stem: A single stock has a high standard deviation and a low beta. What does this combination show?

options.A: Most of its risk is company-specific, not market risk
options.B: Most of its risk comes from market movements
options.C: It has little total risk but high market risk
options.D: It tends to move opposite to the market

questions.rationale: Standard deviation measures total risk, systematic and unsystematic. Beta measures systematic risk only. A high standard deviation with a low beta means that most of the risk is unsystematic.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.3 (exam trap: sigma vs beta)

questions.stem: Returns on a fund are roughly normal. About what share of its annual returns fall within one standard deviation of the mean?

options.A: About 50%
options.B: About 95%
options.C: About 99%
options.D: About 68%

questions.rationale: For roughly normal returns, about 68% of outcomes fall within one standard deviation of the mean. About 95% fall within two standard deviations.

questions.stem: Which statement describes a limit of standard deviation as a risk measure?

options.A: It measures only systematic risk and ignores company risk
options.B: It treats a large gain as risk in the same way as a large loss
options.C: It cannot be calculated for a portfolio of many assets
options.D: It is in squared units, so it cannot be compared to returns

questions.rationale: Standard deviation measures how widely returns scatter around the mean, in both directions. So a large gain counts as risk just like a large loss. It measures total risk, and it is in return units.

questions.stem: A security has a beta of −0.4. How does it tend to behave?

options.A: It tends to move with the market, but by less
options.B: It has no relationship with the market
options.C: It tends to move against the market
options.D: It tends to move more than the market

questions.rationale: The market has a beta of 1. A beta between 0 and 1 means that the security moves with the market, but less. A beta below zero means that it tends to move against the market.

questions.stem: Amadou Sorensen holds a broad, diversified portfolio. He wants to know how much market risk one new stock adds to it. Which measure fits this decision best?

options.A: Beta
options.B: Standard deviation
options.C: Variance
options.D: Maximum drawdown

questions.rationale: Inside a diversified portfolio, the other holdings remove most company-specific risk. So beta, which measures systematic risk, shows the risk that the stock adds. Standard deviation and variance measure total risk.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.3 (beta in a diversified portfolio)

questions.stem: A portfolio has a drawdown from its peak. Which statement about the gain that it needs to return to that peak is correct?

options.A: The gain needed equals the percentage fall
options.B: The gain needed is larger than the percentage fall
options.C: The gain needed is smaller than the percentage fall
options.D: The gain needed depends only on the portfolio's beta

questions.rationale: After the fall, the gain applies to a smaller base. For example, a 25% drawdown needs a gain of about 33% to return to the peak. So the needed gain is larger than the fall.

questions.stem: Corentin Abiola holds 40 Canadian stocks from many sectors. A recession causes the whole market to fall 20%. His portfolio falls about as much. Why did diversification not protect him?

options.A: Diversification cannot remove systematic risk that all stocks share
options.B: He held too few stocks to remove market risk
options.C: Diversification removes only interest rate risk
options.D: Diversification works only for bond portfolios

questions.rationale: Diversification reduces company-specific risk. It cannot remove systematic risk, because all stocks share exposure to the economy. More holdings would not have prevented the market fall.

questions.stem: Wilhelmina Sato has a diversified Canadian equity portfolio. She fears a market fall over the next two months. She does not want to sell. Which action reduces her market risk most directly?

options.A: Take a short position in stock index futures
options.B: Add more Canadian stocks from other sectors
options.C: Buy call options on a Canadian stock index
options.D: Replace low-beta stocks with high-beta stocks

questions.rationale: A hedge takes an offsetting position against one named risk, and it can reduce systematic risk. A short index futures position gains when the market falls. More stocks from the same market cannot remove market risk.

questions.stem: Thandiwe Rousseau holds U.S. stocks in her Canadian-dollar account. She wants to keep the stocks. She fears that the U.S. dollar will fall against the Canadian dollar. Which action fits her concern?

options.A: Add a currency hedge on her U.S. investments
options.B: Buy put options on each of her U.S. stocks
options.C: Sell her U.S. stocks and buy Canadian bonds
options.D: Add more U.S. stocks from other sectors

questions.rationale: A hedge targets one named risk. Her concern is currency risk, not the stocks, so a currency hedge fits. Puts protect against falls in stock prices. A sale removes holdings that she wants to keep.

questions.stem: A portfolio holds 50% in Asset X (standard deviation 20%) and 50% in Asset Y (standard deviation 10%). Their correlation is +0.2. Which statement about the portfolio's standard deviation is correct?

options.A: It is less than 15%
options.B: It is exactly 15%
options.C: It is more than 15%
options.D: It is exactly 20%

questions.rationale: The weighted-average standard deviation is 15%. Portfolio risk is not a weighted average. When the correlation is below +1, portfolio standard deviation is less than the weighted average.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.4 (risk not a weighted average); check sqrt(0.25*400+0.25*100+2*0.25*0.2*200)=12.04%

questions.stem: Two equity funds have a correlation of +1. Linnea Castellanos splits her money equally between them. Which statement about her portfolio is correct?

options.A: Its standard deviation is lower than either fund's
options.B: Its standard deviation equals the average of the two funds
options.C: Its risk can, in theory, be eliminated
options.D: Its expected return is higher than either fund's

questions.rationale: With a correlation of +1, the funds always move together, so there is no risk reduction. Portfolio standard deviation equals the weighted average. Elimination of risk needs a correlation of −1, in theory.

questions.stem: An RR rejects a commodity fund for Oswin Mbeki because the fund's standard deviation alone is high. Its returns have a low correlation with his other holdings. Which reply is most accurate?

options.A: A small weight in the fund can lower his total portfolio risk
options.B: The fund will always raise his total portfolio risk
options.C: The fund's risk alone is the only relevant measure
options.D: The fund will raise his expected return with no added risk

questions.rationale: Judge an asset by how it changes the risk of the whole portfolio, not only by its risk alone. A risky asset with low correlation to the other holdings can lower portfolio risk.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.4 (role of risk in asset selection)

questions.stem: Perpetua Lindgren holds shares of one company. She buys a put option on them with a strike price below the current price. Which statement describes her position until expiry?

options.A: Minimum value of the strike price; the hedge has no cost
options.B: Minimum value of strike less premium; upside kept, less the premium
options.C: Minimum value of the current price; all upside given up
options.D: No minimum value; all upside kept, less the premium

questions.rationale: A protective put gives the right to sell at the strike price until expiry. So it sets a minimum value of the strike less the premium. If the price rises, she keeps the upside, less the premium paid.

questions.stem: Yusuf Brannigan has an open short position in a stock. How does he close (cover) the position?

options.A: He sells more shares, and the dealer cancels the loan
options.B: He deposits cash equal to the original sale price
options.C: He buys the shares, and the dealer returns them to the lender
options.D: He waits until the lender sells the shares for him

questions.rationale: In a short sale, the dealer borrows shares to deliver to the buyer. To cover, the client buys the shares back, and the dealer returns them to the lender. A cash deposit does not return the shares.

questions.stem: A Participant enters an order to sell shares for a client. On execution, the sale will be a short sale. The order is not a short-marking exempt order. What does UMIR 3.2 require?

options.A: The order must be held until the trade settles
options.B: The order must be entered as a limit order only
options.C: The order needs no marking if the client has a margin account
options.D: The order must be marked as a short sale

questions.rationale: Under UMIR 3.2(1), a Participant must not enter a short-sale order on a marketplace unless the order is marked short. Only short-marking exempt orders are excepted. A margin account does not remove this duty.
questions.source_quote: "unless the order is marked as a short sale in accordance with subclause 6.2(1)(b)(viii)" — research/sources/ciro/umir-2026-08-11.txt UMIR 3.2(1)(a), ~line 5438

questions.stem: The Market Regulator has designated a stock as a Short Sale Ineligible Security for today. Ottilie Faraday asks her dealer to sell it short today. What does UMIR 3.2 provide?

options.A: The Participant may enter the order if it is marked short
options.B: The Participant must not enter the order, subject to limited exceptions
options.C: The Participant may enter the order if it arranges a borrow first
options.D: The Participant may enter the order at a price above the last sale

questions.rationale: UMIR 3.2(1) bars a short-sale order if the security is a Short Sale Ineligible Security at the time of entry. Only the exceptions in UMIR 3.2(3) apply. A prior borrow is the condition for a Pre-Borrow Security.
questions.source_quote: "if the security is a Short Sale Ineligible Security at the time of the entry of the order" — research/sources/ciro/umir-2026-08-11.txt UMIR 3.2(1)(b), ~line 5441

questions.stem: A stock is designated as a Pre-Borrow Security. A Participant wants to enter a short-sale order in it for a client. When may the Participant enter the order?

options.A: Only after the trade settles and the shares are delivered
options.B: At any time, if the order is marked as a short sale
options.C: Only after it arranges to borrow the shares needed for settlement
options.D: Never, because the rules bar all short sales in the stock

questions.rationale: For a Pre-Borrow Security, UMIR 3.2(1) permits a short-sale order only if the Participant arranged the borrowing before it entered the order. Marking alone is not enough. A full bar applies to a Short Sale Ineligible Security.
questions.source_quote: "has made arrangements for the borrowing of the securities necessary to settle any resulting trade prior to the entry of the order" — research/sources/ciro/umir-2026-08-11.txt UMIR 3.2(1)(c), ~line 5443

questions.stem: Rafferty Nkemelu does not own a stock. His dealer arranges to borrow the shares for him, and he then sells them. How does UMIR treat this sale?

options.A: It is not a short sale, because he has the shares to deliver
options.B: It is not a short sale, because the borrow was arranged first
options.C: It is a short sale only if the price later rises
options.D: It is a short sale, because borrowed shares do not count as owned

questions.rationale: A UMIR short sale is a sale of a security that the seller does not own. A seller who borrowed the security for delivery is not considered to own it. So a sale of borrowed shares is a short sale.
questions.source_quote: "the seller has borrowed the security to be delivered on the settlement of the trade and the seller is not otherwise considered to own the security in accordance with this definition" — research/sources/ciro/umir-2026-08-11.txt UMIR 1.1 "short sale" (f), ~line 2482

questions.stem: Cosimo Albrecht holds a short position. The lender of the shares asks for them back. No other shares are available to borrow. Which short-sale risk does this show?

options.A: Short-squeeze risk, from many short sellers covering at once
options.B: Recall risk, which can force a cover at a bad time
options.C: Carry-cost risk, from dividends on the borrowed shares
options.D: Margin-call risk, from a rise in the share price

questions.rationale: The lender can ask for the shares back. If no other shares are available, the client must cover, possibly at a bad time. A short squeeze needs many short sellers to cover at once.

questions.stem: Ingrid Valcourt is short a stock. The company pays a dividend while her position is open. What effect does the dividend have on her?

options.A: She receives the dividend because she sold the shares
options.B: The dividend goes to the buyer, so it has no effect on her
options.C: She pays the dividend amount on the borrowed shares
options.D: The dividend reduces her margin requirement on the position

questions.rationale: While a short position is open, the client pays any dividends and borrowing fees on the borrowed shares. These carry costs reduce her profit. She does not receive the dividend, because she does not own the shares.

questions.stem: Zuzanna Eklund is short a volatile stock. She wants a firm maximum on her loss, and she accepts a cost for it. Which action fits best?

options.A: Place a stop-buy order above the current price
options.B: Buy a put option on the stock
options.C: Sell more shares short at a higher price
options.D: Buy a call option on the stock

questions.rationale: A call option sets a maximum loss, but it costs a premium. A stop-buy order can limit the loss. But if the stock opens much higher, the loss can be larger than the stop price suggests.

questions.stem: Anselm Okoro sells short a margin-eligible stock listed on a Canadian exchange. The stock trades at $0.20 per share. What is the minimum client margin requirement?

options.A: $0.25 per share
options.B: 100% of market value
options.C: 80% of market value
options.D: 50% of market value

questions.rationale: For short positions, the IDPC 5310 table sets $0.25 per share when the price is below $0.25. A long position at that price has a 100% rate. The 80% rate applies from $1.50 to $1.74.
questions.source_quote: "Market value of below $0.25 per share $0.25 per share" — research/sources/ciro/idpc-rules-2026-08-11.txt IDPC 5310(1) short table, ~line 16196

questions.stem: Mireille Okonjo's margin account becomes undermargined after a price move. Before she fixes the deficiency, she asks to withdraw $5,000 in cash. What must the dealer do?

options.A: Permit it if she fixes the deficiency within 20 business days
options.B: Refuse the withdrawal while the account is undermargined
options.C: Permit it if the amount is under 10% of the account value
options.D: Permit it and issue a margin call for the same amount

questions.rationale: Form 1, Schedule 4, Note 5 bars advancing funds or delivering securities while the account is undermargined. The 20-business-day period applies to restricting the account to trades that reduce the deficiency.
questions.source_quote: "Advancing funds or delivering securities from the account of a customer shall not be permitted as long as the account is undermargined or if such advance or delivery would cause the account to become undermargined." — research/sources/ciro/idpc-form-1-schedule-4-cash-and-margin-accounts.txt Form 1 Sch. 4 Note 5(iv), ~line 114

questions.stem: Lior Haddad is short a stock in his margin account. The price rises sharply, and he is now indebted to the dealer. The dealer considers action necessary for its credit risk protection. What may it do?

options.A: Lend him more shares to extend the position
options.B: Freeze the account but take no trading action
options.C: Cancel the short sale and reverse the trade
options.D: Buy the securities that Lior holds short

questions.rationale: IDPC 5116 lets a dealer buy securities held short for an indebted client when it considers this necessary for its credit risk protection. The margin agreement must describe this right to cover short sales.
questions.source_quote: "buy securities held short for an indebted client" — research/sources/ciro/idpc-rules-2026-08-11.txt IDPC 5116(1)(i), ~line 14822

questions.stem: Bjorn Tveit sells a stock short in his margin account and receives $10,000 in proceeds. He asks to withdraw the $10,000. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The proceeds stay in the account as part of the required credit
options.B: He may withdraw the proceeds because the sale has settled
options.C: He may withdraw half, because the margin rate is 50%
options.D: He may withdraw them if he enters a stop-buy order

questions.rationale: A short position needs a credit balance at least equal to its net negative loan value. At a 50% rate, that credit is 150% of the shares' value. So the proceeds stay in the account and are not free cash.
questions.source_quote: "the cash balance in the margin account must be a credit equal to or larger than the net negative loan value for the account to be in good standing" — research/sources/ciro/idpc-rules-2026-08-11.txt IDPC 5113(4)(iii), ~line 14796

questions.stem: A portfolio plots below the efficient frontier. What does this position show?

options.A: The portfolio has the lowest risk of all possible portfolios
options.B: The portfolio suits only investors with a high risk tolerance
options.C: Another portfolio gives a higher expected return for the same risk
options.D: The portfolio has no unsystematic risk left in it

questions.rationale: The efficient frontier is the set of portfolios with the highest expected return for each level of risk. A portfolio below it is inefficient, because another portfolio gives more return for the same risk.

questions.stem: Which statement describes a main weakness of plain mean–variance optimization?

options.A: It ignores the correlations between the assets
options.B: It assumes that investors prefer more risk
options.C: It needs no estimate of expected returns
options.D: Small errors in its estimates can change the weights a lot

questions.rationale: MPT needs an expected return, a standard deviation and correlations for each asset. Small errors in these estimates can change the weights a lot, often to extreme ones. MPT assumes that investors are risk averse.

questions.stem: Two portfolios each hold 20 assets. One uses equal weights. The other picks weights from estimates of return, risk and correlation. What is the main advantage of the second approach?

options.A: It removes all systematic risk from the portfolio
options.B: It gets more risk reduction per holding by using correlations
options.C: It guarantees a higher return than equal weights
options.D: It needs no estimates of the assets' returns

questions.rationale: Efficient diversification chooses weights from expected return, standard deviation and correlation. It seeks low-correlation assets, so it gets more risk reduction per holding than equal weights. No diversification removes systematic risk.

questions.stem: A Monte Carlo simulation reports an 82% probability that Gwendolyn Oyelaran's savings last to age 92. What does this result also show?

options.A: Her savings are certain to last to age 92
options.B: The savings run out before age 92 in about 18% of the paths
options.C: Her savings last to age 82 in every path
options.D: Her portfolio earns 82% of its expected return

questions.rationale: Monte Carlo runs thousands of random return paths and reports a distribution of outcomes. An 82% success rate means that the savings run out in about 18% of the paths. It gives probabilities, not a guarantee.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the main limit of the Black–Litterman model?

options.A: It always gives extreme, concentrated weights
options.B: It ignores market-capitalization weights
options.C: Its result depends on the views and confidence levels that the manager enters
options.D: It cannot include any views of the manager

questions.rationale: Black–Litterman blends the manager's views, weighted by confidence, into market equilibrium returns. This gives more stable weights than plain optimization. But poor views or confidence levels still give a poor portfolio.

questions.stem: Which task is a main purpose of an asset pricing model?

options.A: To calculate a fund's management expense ratio
options.B: To set the discount rate used to value a security
options.C: To measure the largest fall from a peak to a later low
options.D: To set the client's time horizon and liquidity needs

questions.rationale: An asset pricing model estimates the return that investors require for an asset's risk. Managers use that return as a discount rate, to judge fair price and to test alpha. Time horizon and liquidity come from the client's KYC information. Drawdown is a risk measure.

questions.stem: Why does the CAPM give a reward only for systematic risk?

options.A: Systematic risk is always larger than unsystematic risk
options.B: Standard deviation cannot measure unsystematic risk
options.C: Investors can remove unsystematic risk by diversification at no cost
options.D: Regulators require models to ignore company-specific risk

questions.rationale: In the CAPM, diversification removes unsystematic risk at no cost, so the market pays no premium for it. Only beta, the exposure to market risk, earns a reward. The relative size of the two risks is not the reason.

questions.stem: Which statement describes a disadvantage of the CAPM?

options.A: The true market portfolio that it needs cannot be observed
options.B: It does not say which factors or how many factors to use
options.C: It needs data on size, value, profitability and investment
options.D: It rewards unsystematic risk that diversification can remove

questions.rationale: The CAPM needs the true market portfolio, which no one can observe. Its other weaknesses are unrealistic assumptions and a single beta that often explains returns poorly. The failure to name the factors is a weakness of the APT, not of the CAPM.

questions.stem: Gisela Castellano prefers arbitrage pricing theory (APT) to the CAPM, because the APT needs fewer assumptions. Which drawback of the APT must she accept?

options.A: The theory needs the true market portfolio, which no one can observe
options.B: The theory does not name the factors or say how many to use
options.C: The theory allows only one factor, which is beta to the market
options.D: The theory adds momentum, which is volatile and costly to trade

questions.rationale: The APT explains return with several systematic factors but does not name them or their number. So the choice of factors is subjective. An unobservable market portfolio is a CAPM weakness. Costly momentum trading is a weakness of the Carhart model.

questions.stem: Two well-diversified portfolios have the same exposures to inflation, GDP growth and interest rates. Under arbitrage pricing theory, what must be true?

options.A: The portfolio with more holdings must have the higher expected return
options.B: Their expected returns can differ because of their unsystematic risk
options.C: The portfolio with the lower price must have the lower expected return
options.D: They must have the same expected return

questions.rationale: The APT rests on no-arbitrage. Portfolios with the same factor exposures must have the same expected return. Otherwise, traders could buy one, sell the other and earn a riskless profit. Unsystematic risk earns no extra return.

questions.stem: Which factor is in the Fama–French five-factor model but not in the Carhart four-factor model?

options.A: Momentum (winners minus losers)
options.B: Profitability (robust minus weak)
options.C: Value (high minus low)
options.D: Size (small minus big)

questions.rationale: Carhart uses the market, size and value factors plus momentum. The Fama–French five-factor model uses market, size and value plus profitability and investment. So profitability is only in the five-factor model. Momentum is only in Carhart, and size and value are in both.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.7 multi-factor table and exam trap

questions.stem: A researcher adds a momentum factor to the Fama–French five-factor model. Which statement about the new model is correct?

options.A: It has four factors and is the same as the Carhart model
options.B: It has six factors and is the simplest multi-factor model
options.C: It has five factors, because momentum replaces investment
options.D: It has six factors and the greatest risk of data-mining

questions.rationale: Five factors plus momentum give six factors. This model covers the most known anomalies, but it is the most complex and has the greatest risk of data-mining. The Carhart model has four factors: the three original Fama–French factors plus momentum.

questions.stem: In a multi-factor model, what does the value factor (HML) measure?

options.A: Returns of high book-to-market stocks minus low book-to-market stocks
options.B: Returns of firms with robust profitability minus firms with weak profitability
options.C: Returns of stocks with high recent returns minus those with low recent returns
options.D: Returns of large companies minus returns of small companies

questions.rationale: HML means high minus low book-to-market, so it compares cheap (value) stocks with expensive ones. Winners minus losers is the momentum factor. Robust minus weak profitability is RMW. The size factor is small minus big, not large minus small.

questions.stem: Use a T-bill yield of 3.5% and a market risk premium of 6%. Shares of Norlake Corp. have a beta of 1.25. What return does the CAPM require for them?
questions.rationale: Required return = 3.5% + 1.25 × 6% = 11.0%. The premium is already given, so do not subtract the risk-free rate again. The 7.5% result omits the risk-free rate. The 9.5% result ignores beta.

questions.stem: Vasco Lombardi's analyst forecasts an 11.5% return for a stock with a beta of 1.6. T-bills yield 2%, and the market should return 7%. What should Vasco conclude?

options.A: Alpha is −1.5%, so the stock is overvalued
options.B: Alpha is −1.7%, so the stock is overvalued
options.C: Alpha is +1.5%, so the stock is undervalued
options.D: Alpha is +0.3%, so the stock is fairly priced

questions.rationale: The CAPM return is 2% + 1.6 × (7% − 2%) = 10.0%. The forecast is 1.5% higher, so the stock plots above the SML and is undervalued. The +0.3% result multiplies beta by the market return, not by the premium.

questions.stem: Tavish Vandermeer splits his money: 30% in a stock (beta 1.4), 50% in an equity fund (beta 1.0) and 20% in T-bills. What is his portfolio's beta?
questions.rationale: Portfolio beta is the weighted average: 0.3 × 1.4 + 0.5 × 1.0 + 0.2 × 0 = 0.92. T-bills have a beta of zero but still count in the weights. The 0.80 result is a simple average, and 1.15 leaves the T-bills out.

questions.stem: An analyst says that a stock must return 12% to compensate for its risk under the CAPM. T-bills yield 3%, and the market should return 9%. What beta does this imply?
questions.rationale: Solve 12% = 3% + β × (9% − 3%). So β = 9% ÷ 6% = 1.50. The 1.33 result divides 12% by the market return. The 1.00 result divides the 9% excess return by the market return instead of by the premium.

questions.stem: Yannick Abelard wants a CAPM expected return of 7%. He will mix a market index fund (beta 1.0) with T-bills. T-bills yield 3%, and the market should return 8%. What weight goes in the index fund?
questions.rationale: He needs a beta of (7% − 3%) ÷ (8% − 3%) = 0.80. The index fund has a beta of 1.0 and T-bills have a beta of zero, so 80% goes in the fund. The 87.5% result divides 7% by 8%. The 20% result is the T-bill weight.

questions.stem: Ulla Ferreiro wants a higher CAPM expected return for her portfolio. The risk-free rate and the expected market return stay the same. What must she accept?

options.A: A higher portfolio beta, which means more market risk
options.B: A higher standard deviation with the same beta
options.C: A larger share of T-bills in her portfolio
options.D: More unsystematic risk from fewer holdings

questions.rationale: In the CAPM, expected return rises only with beta, so she must accept more market risk. The CAPM pays nothing for unsystematic risk or for volatility that does not come from beta. More T-bills lower beta and so lower the expected return.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.8 expected return and risk of a portfolio

questions.stem: T-bills yield 3%, and the market should return 8%. Stock X has a standard deviation of 45% and a beta of 0.4. Stock Y has a standard deviation of 20% and a beta of 1.3. Which stock has the higher CAPM required return?

options.A: Stock Y, because a lower standard deviation always earns more
options.B: Neither, because both must return only the 3% risk-free rate
options.C: Stock X, because the CAPM rewards its higher standard deviation
options.D: Stock Y, at 9.5%, because the CAPM prices only beta

questions.rationale: Stock X requires 3% + 0.4 × 5% = 5.0%. Stock Y requires 3% + 1.3 × 5% = 9.5%. The CAPM rewards only systematic risk, which beta measures. Most of Stock X's high volatility is unsystematic, and diversification can remove it.

questions.stem: T-bills yield 4%, and the market should return 9%. Which stock below is undervalued under the CAPM?

options.A: Stock S: beta 1.0, forecast return 8.5%
options.B: Stock R: beta 1.5, forecast return 11.0%
options.C: Stock Q: beta 0.6, forecast return 8.0%
options.D: Stock P: beta 1.2, forecast return 10.0%

questions.rationale: Required returns are 4% + β × 5%: P 10.0%, Q 7.0%, R 11.5% and S 9.0%. Only Stock Q has a forecast above its required return, so it plots above the SML. Stock P plots on the SML. Stocks R and S plot below it.
questions.qa_note: calc: required = 4 + b x 5 -> P 10.0 (fcst 10.0), Q 7.0 (fcst 8.0), R 11.5 (fcst 11.0), S 9.0 (fcst 8.5)

questions.stem: Bronwen Tallis puts half her money in an index fund (beta 1.0), 30% in a stock (beta 1.6) and the rest in T-bills. T-bills yield 2.5%, and the market should return 8.5%. What is her CAPM expected return?
questions.rationale: Portfolio beta = 0.5 × 1.0 + 0.3 × 1.6 + 0.2 × 0 = 0.98. Expected return = 2.5% + 0.98 × 6% = 8.38%. The 5.88% result omits the risk-free rate. The 10.83% result multiplies beta by the market return, not by the premium.

questions.stem: Under weak-form efficiency, which information do market prices already reflect?

options.A: All past price and volume data
options.B: All public information, including financial statements
options.C: All information, both public and private
options.D: Only the information in company press releases

questions.rationale: Weak-form efficiency means that prices reflect all past price and volume data, so technical analysis cannot earn abnormal returns. The semi-strong form adds all public information. The strong form adds private information too.

questions.stem: Suppose a market is strong-form efficient. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Only insider information can give consistent abnormal returns
options.B: Only fundamental analysis of public data can give abnormal returns
options.C: Technical analysis can give abnormal returns, but fundamental analysis cannot
options.D: Not even insider information can give consistent abnormal returns

questions.rationale: Strong-form prices reflect all information, public and private, so no information gives an edge. Insider information gives an edge only if the market is semi-strong but not strong-form efficient. The strong form includes the weaker forms, so technical and fundamental analysis also fail.

questions.stem: Henrik Brannock buys software that finds buy signals in past stock prices and trading volume. The market is weak-form efficient. What should he expect?

options.A: Lower risk, because the signals avoid all market declines
options.B: No abnormal returns, but lower costs than an index fund
options.C: Consistent abnormal returns, because the software is faster than analysts
options.D: No consistent abnormal returns, and higher trading costs

questions.rationale: Weak-form efficiency means that prices already reflect past price and volume data. So signals from those data cannot give consistent abnormal returns. Each extra trade adds spreads and commissions, so his costs rise above those of a low-cost index fund.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.9 weak form; chart-pattern scenario

questions.stem: Petra Hargreaves believes that large Canadian stocks are close to semi-strong efficient. Which approach best fits this belief for her core holdings?

options.A: A fund that rotates sectors on public economic forecasts
options.B: A fund that picks stocks from public financial statements
options.C: A low-cost fund that tracks a broad index
options.D: A fund that trades on chart patterns each week

questions.rationale: In a semi-strong efficient market, prices adjust quickly to all public information. Research on public data is then unlikely to earn more than its cost. So the EMH favours passive, low-cost indexing. The other funds rely on public data that prices already reflect.

questions.stem: Suppose markets are efficient. How can a portfolio manager still add value for a client?

options.A: By setting the asset mix and controlling costs and taxes
options.B: By moving to cash when chart signals show a peak
options.C: By buying the funds with the best returns last year
options.D: By picking stocks that look cheap in published reports

questions.rationale: If prices already reflect information, security selection is unlikely to beat its cost. The manager adds value in other ways: set the asset mix, manage risk, control costs and taxes, and fit the portfolio to the client. Published reports and charts are data that prices already reflect.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.9 implications for portfolio management

questions.stem: According to the EMH, why are future price changes hard to predict?

options.A: Prices change only on private information that the public never sees
options.B: New information arrives at random, and competing analysts quickly move prices to fair value
options.C: Most investors ignore news, so prices drift slowly toward fair value over time
options.D: Regulators stop analysts from trading on new public information until it is old

questions.rationale: The EMH rests on competition. Many analysts search for mispriced securities, and their trades quickly move prices to fair value. New information arrives at random, so the next price change is hard to predict. A slow drift would make prices predictable.

questions.stem: Where does the evidence suggest that active managers have the most room to add value?

options.A: In less-followed segments, such as small-cap stocks
options.B: In large stocks that many analysts follow closely
options.C: In markets that are strong-form efficient
options.D: In the stocks with the most daily news coverage

questions.rationale: Most observers see large, heavily followed markets as close to semi-strong efficient. Fewer analysts follow small caps and some bonds, so these segments may leave more room for active managers. In a strong-form efficient market, no information gives an edge.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.9 limits of the EMH

questions.stem: Yorick Haverford starts with a forecast of strong GDP growth. Next, he picks the sectors likely to gain most. Last, he picks companies in those sectors. Which weakness is most specific to his approach?

options.A: He can pay a premium for growth that later slows
options.B: He can overlook sector and economic risk in his holdings
options.C: He can buy cheap stocks whose businesses are in permanent decline
options.D: He can miss good companies in the sectors that he does not favour

questions.rationale: Economy first, then sectors, then companies is a top-down approach. Top-down captures macro and sector trends, but it can miss good companies in the wrong sectors. Overlooking sector or economic risk is the typical weakness of a bottom-up manager.

questions.stem: Winnie Sandoval picks 20 stocks only on company fundamentals and pays little attention to the economy. Later, 65% of her fund is in one sector. Which risk does this show?

options.A: Cap-weighted indexing concentrates in the largest companies
options.B: Market timing needs two correct forecasts to succeed
options.C: Bottom-up selection can overlook sector and economic risk
options.D: Top-down selection can miss good companies in weak sectors

questions.rationale: Winnie studies companies first, so she is a bottom-up manager. Bottom-up finds individual mispricings but can overlook sector or macro risk. Here her stock choices built a large sector bet that she did not plan. Missing good companies in weak sectors is the top-down weakness.

questions.stem: Rafferty Montague expects the economy to enter a contraction. He keeps his fund fully invested in equities but moves into consumer staples, utilities and health care. Which technique does he use?

options.A: Buy and hold
options.B: Market timing
options.C: Sector rotation
options.D: Value investing

questions.rationale: Rafferty overweights the sectors that he expects to lead in the next phase of the cycle, so he uses sector rotation. Defensive sectors fit a contraction. He is not a market timer, because he does not switch out of equities into cash or bonds.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.10 sector rotation vs market timing

questions.stem: Which list matches the common textbook pattern of sector rotation over the business cycle?

options.A: Early expansion: energy; late expansion: utilities; contraction: financials
options.B: Early expansion: utilities; late expansion: financials; contraction: energy
options.C: Early expansion: financials; late expansion: energy; contraction: utilities
options.D: Early expansion: financials; late expansion: utilities; contraction: energy

questions.rationale: In the textbook pattern, cyclicals such as consumer discretionary and financials lead in early expansion. Energy and materials lead in late expansion. Defensives such as staples, utilities and health care lead in contraction. Actual leadership varies from cycle to cycle.

questions.stem: Dov Szymanski buys a stock with a P/E ratio of 4 and a dividend yield of 9%. A new technology is replacing the company's main product. Which risk matters most here?

options.A: Growth risk: both earnings and a high P/E multiple can fall at the same time
options.B: Timing risk: he must be right about both the exit and the re-entry
options.C: A value trap: the stock is cheap because its business is in permanent decline
options.D: Tracking error: the stock can move differently from its benchmark index

questions.rationale: A low P/E and a high yield make this a value purchase. The main danger in value investing is a value trap, a stock that is cheap because its business is in permanent decline. A falling high P/E is a growth-stock risk, and this multiple is already low.

questions.stem: Which pair of traits is most typical of the stocks that a growth manager buys?

options.A: Low P/E ratios and high dividend yields
options.B: Low P/E ratios and low earnings growth
options.C: High P/E ratios and low dividend yields
options.D: Low price-to-book ratios and high dividend yields

questions.rationale: Growth managers buy companies with above-average earnings growth. Their prices already include that growth, so P/E ratios are high, and their dividends are often low. Low P/E, low price-to-book and high dividend yield are value traits.

questions.stem: Two managers act on the same forecast. Eulalie Drummond raises equities from 60% to 65%, inside her policy range. Umberto Quarles cuts equities from 80% to 20% and holds cash. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Both make tactical tilts, because both keep some equities
options.B: Umberto is a market timer, and Eulalie makes a tactical tilt
options.C: Both are market timers, because both act on a forecast
options.D: Eulalie is a market timer, and Umberto makes a tactical tilt

questions.rationale: Market timing is the extreme form of tactical allocation: large switches between equities and cash on market forecasts. A tactical tilt is a smaller move inside set ranges around the strategic mix. Both moves use a forecast, so the size and the range decide the label.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.10 market timing vs tactical allocation

questions.stem: Xiomara Underhill moved her equities to cash before a market fall. She will wait for clear signs of recovery before she buys again. Why can this cost her much of her long-run return?

options.A: She can miss a few very strong days, which give a large part of long-run returns
options.B: Recoveries are always slower than the falls that come before them
options.C: Cash always loses value faster than equities lose value during a market fall
options.D: Equities pay no dividends during a recovery, so she loses no income by waiting

questions.rationale: Out of the market, a timer can miss a few very strong days, and those days give a large part of long-run returns. If she waits for clear signs of recovery, she can be in cash on those days. This risk adds to the risk of a wrong exit.

questions.stem: Valka Prentice says: "I am a value manager, so I must use a bottom-up process." Which reply is correct?

options.A: Incorrect: value is a style, which a manager can run top-down or bottom-up
options.B: Incorrect: value managers must always start with an economic forecast
options.C: Correct: value managers must study company ratios before the economy
options.D: Correct: only growth managers can use a top-down process

questions.rationale: Growth and value are styles. Top-down and bottom-up describe the order of analysis. A manager can combine either style with either approach. So a value manager can choose favoured sectors first and then buy the cheapest companies in them.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a buy-and-hold portfolio from an index portfolio?

options.A: The buy-and-hold portfolio has high turnover; the index portfolio has none
options.B: The buy-and-hold manager chose the securities; the index manager copies a benchmark
options.C: The buy-and-hold manager rebalances to targets; the index manager never trades
options.D: The buy-and-hold portfolio has no market risk; the index portfolio has full market risk

questions.rationale: Both are passive and trade little. But a buy-and-hold manager still selected the original securities, while an index manager copies a benchmark such as the S&P/TSX Composite. A buy-and-hold manager does not rebalance, so the mix drifts. Both carry market risk.

questions.stem: Folasade Eriksen bought 12 stocks 18 years ago and never traded or rebalanced. One stock is now 35% of her portfolio. Which statement best describes her risk?

options.A: Her risk now equals the risk of a broad market index
options.B: Her risk has drifted into a large concentration in one issuer
options.C: Her risk is unchanged, because she still holds the same 12 stocks
options.D: Her risk is low, because buy and hold removes market risk

questions.rationale: Without rebalancing, a buy-and-hold mix drifts, so its risk changes over time. The best performer grew to 35%, which is an issuer concentration. The same names do not keep the same weights or risk. Buy and hold does not remove market risk.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.11 buy and hold drift

questions.stem: An index fund holds 140 of the 220 stocks in its index. The manager chose them as a representative subset and uses no optimization model. Which indexing method is this?

options.A: Optimization
options.B: Full replication
options.C: Sector rotation
options.D: Sampling

questions.rationale: Sampling holds a representative subset of the index. Full replication holds every index stock at its index weight. Optimization uses a model to minimize the deviation from the index. Sector rotation is an active technique, not an indexing method.

questions.stem: An index ETF trails its index by close to the same amount every year. Which cause best explains most of this tracking difference?

options.A: The timing of trades during the year
options.B: Cash drag that changes with fund flows
options.C: Sampling of the index stocks
options.D: The fund's fees

questions.rationale: Fees reduce the return by about the same amount each year, so they cause most of the tracking difference. Sampling, cash drag and trade timing have effects that change from period to period. They cause most of the tracking error.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.11 tracking difference vs tracking error

questions.stem: An index fund's return gap with its index swings between −0.6% and +0.5% from month to month. On average, the gap is small. Which cause best fits this pattern?

options.A: The fund holds only a sample of the index stocks
options.B: The fund carries full market risk, like its index
options.C: The fund's index is weighted by market capitalization
options.D: The fund charges a fixed annual management fee

questions.rationale: A gap that changes a lot but is small on average shows high tracking error, not a large tracking difference. Sampling, cash drag and trade timing cause most tracking error. A steady fee mainly causes a steady tracking difference. Market risk affects the fund and the index alike.

questions.stem: Ansel Jankowski holds a cap-weighted Canadian equity index fund. He sees that a few sectors and the largest stocks make up much of the fund. Which disadvantage of indexing does this show?

options.A: Index funds carry security-selection risk from manager choices
options.B: Cap weighting concentrates the fund in the largest stocks and sectors
options.C: Full replication increases tracking error over time
options.D: Index funds have high turnover and poor tax efficiency

questions.rationale: A cap-weighted index gives the most weight to the largest companies, which are sometimes overvalued. So the fund can concentrate in a few stocks or sectors. Indexing has low turnover and good tax efficiency, and it largely removes security-selection risk.

questions.stem: Hedda Yamamoto wants an index fund that beats the S&P/TSX Composite in rising markets. Which reply is accurate?

options.A: The fund beats the index if it uses full replication
options.B: The fund beats the index in rising markets because its fees are low
options.C: The fund's return is capped at the index return less costs
options.D: The fund can beat the index whenever its tracking error is high

questions.rationale: Passive management accepts the market return and does not try to beat it. The index return less costs is the ceiling. Low fees narrow the gap but do not lift the fund above the index. High tracking error means less consistent tracking, not a reliable gain.

questions.stem: A bond manager expects interest rates to rise. Which step fits this forecast?

options.A: Move into long-term strip bonds
options.B: Set duration equal to the client's horizon
options.C: Lengthen the portfolio's duration
options.D: Shorten the portfolio's duration

questions.rationale: Bond prices fall when rates rise, and a longer duration means a larger price fall. So a manager who expects higher rates shortens duration. Long strip bonds lengthen duration. Matching duration to a horizon is immunization, a passive technique with no rate forecast.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.12 duration management and exam trap

questions.stem: A manager lengthens duration because she expects interest rates to fall. Instead, rates rise. What is the result?

options.A: Prices rise, because longer bonds pay higher coupons
options.B: Higher reinvestment income fully offsets the price loss
options.C: Nothing changes, because duration affects only cash flows
options.D: Prices fall more than they would have at the old duration

questions.rationale: Duration management gains if the rate forecast is right and loses more if it is wrong. With a longer duration, a rise in rates causes a larger price fall than at the old duration. A full offset from reinvestment income is the aim of immunization, not of a rate bet.

questions.stem: A manager sells a bond and buys a nearly identical bond that offers a slightly higher yield. Which technique is this?

options.A: A substitution swap
options.B: Immunization
options.C: A rate anticipation swap
options.D: An intermarket spread swap

questions.rationale: A substitution swap exchanges a bond for a near-identical bond at a better yield. A rate anticipation swap changes maturity or duration to match a rate forecast. An intermarket swap moves between sectors when a spread looks too wide or too narrow.

questions.stem: Mattias Fairweather sells a bond at a capital loss in a tax-loss swap. He wants similar exposure and a deductible loss. Which replacement fits?

options.A: The identical bond, bought 25 days before the sale and still held
options.B: The identical bond, bought by his spouse 10 days after the sale
options.C: The identical bond, bought back 20 days after the sale
options.D: A similar but not identical bond, bought right after the sale

questions.rationale: A tax-loss swap buys a similar, not identical, bond. The superficial loss rule denies the loss if he or an affiliated person buys identical property within 30 days before or after the sale. A spouse is an affiliated person.
questions.source_quote: "You, or a person affiliated with you, buys, or has a right to buy, the same or identical property" — research/sources/cra/capital-gains-losses-superficial-loss-pages.txt CRA superficial loss page, ~line 728
questions.qa_note: regulatory: guide 6.12 tax-loss swap; 7.9 conditions (affiliated incl. spouse)

questions.stem: A manager thinks that the yield spread between provincial and corporate bonds is too wide. She sells provincial bonds and buys corporate bonds. Which swap is this?

options.A: An intermarket (yield-spread) swap
options.B: A rate anticipation swap
options.C: A tax-loss swap
options.D: A substitution swap

questions.rationale: An intermarket swap moves between bond sectors when a spread looks too wide or too narrow. She expects the spread to narrow, so corporates should gain against provincials. A substitution swap uses a near-identical bond, and a rate anticipation swap acts on a rate forecast.

questions.stem: A bond index holds too many issues for a manager to buy them all. How does an index-matching manager usually build the portfolio?

options.A: Hold only the index's largest issues, whatever their duration
options.B: Hold a sample that matches the index's duration, sector and credit quality
options.C: Hold a ladder of bonds with staggered maturities to the horizon
options.D: Set the portfolio's duration equal to the client's horizon

questions.rationale: Index matching copies a bond index at low cost. The index holds too many issues, so the manager holds a sample that matches it in duration, sector and credit quality. The main risk is tracking error. A ladder is buy and hold, and horizon matching is immunization.

questions.stem: A portfolio is immunized for a five-year horizon. Interest rates then rise. What offsets the fall in bond prices?

options.A: A matching rise in the bonds' par values
options.B: Higher income from reinvesting coupons at the new rates
options.C: Higher prices on the longer bonds in the portfolio
options.D: A rise in the portfolio's credit quality

questions.rationale: Immunization sets the portfolio's Macaulay duration equal to the horizon. If rates rise, prices fall, but coupons are reinvested at higher rates. If rates fall, higher prices offset the lower reinvestment income. Par values do not change, and longer bonds fall most when rates rise.

questions.stem: Zelda Calloway holds a ladder of corporate bonds to maturity. She believes that she will get par back on every bond. Which risk can make her wrong?

options.A: Interest rate risk
options.B: Issuer (credit) risk
options.C: Reinvestment risk
options.D: Inflation risk

questions.rationale: Held to maturity, each bond repays par whatever the level of interest rates. Reinvestment risk affects the rate on the money that matures, and inflation affects its buying power. But if an issuer defaults, she does not get par back. A ladder keeps issuer risk.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.12 buy and hold ladder

questions.stem: Rosalind Okafor is 59 and plans to retire in two years. She says she enjoys market swings. Her savings are small compared with her retirement needs. Which risk profile should her RR record?

options.A: A high risk profile, because her stated willingness to accept risk decides the profile
options.B: A medium risk profile, because the RR averages her risk tolerance and her risk capacity
options.C: A low risk profile, because the profile reflects the lower of her risk tolerance and risk capacity
options.D: A high risk profile, because her retirement goal needs a higher return than her savings earn
