options.A: The RR acts correctly, because a fast decision reduces market risk
options.B: The RR acts incorrectly, because the commitment must follow her understanding
options.C: The RR acts correctly if the RR documents the date of her decision
options.D: The RR acts incorrectly only if the product has a deferred sales charge

questions.rationale: The RR must not put pressure on the client. The RR gets the commitment only after the client understands the recommendation. Documentation does not correct a commitment obtained under pressure.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 7.7 (do not put pressure on the client; commitment only after understanding)

questions.stem: Teodora Vlasic needs $30,000 in 6 years for a known liability. She can earn 4% a year, compounded annually. She will make equal deposits at the end of each year. What deposit does she need each year?
questions.rationale: PMT = FV × r ÷ ((1 + r)^n − 1) = 30,000 × 0.04 ÷ (1.04^6 − 1) = $4,522.86. $5,000 ignores interest. $4,348.90 assumes deposits at the start of each year.

questions.stem: Casimir Nowak invests $120,000 at 6% a year, compounded annually. He wants equal payments at the end of each year for 10 years. The balance is zero after the last payment. What is each payment?
questions.rationale: PMT = PV × r ÷ (1 − (1 + r)^−n) = 120,000 × 0.06 ÷ (1 − 1.06^−10) = $16,304.15. $15,381.28 is the payment if payments start immediately. $12,000 ignores interest.

questions.stem: Ingeborg Falk invests $200,000 at a nominal 6% a year, compounded monthly. She wants equal payments at the end of each month for 20 years. The balance is zero after the last payment. What is each monthly payment?
questions.rationale: Use r = 0.06 ÷ 12 = 0.005 and n = 20 × 12 = 240. PMT = 200,000 × 0.005 ÷ (1 − 1.005^−240) = $1,432.86. $1,453.08 is the annual payment divided by 12, which uses the wrong period.

questions.stem: Gaspard Lemaire is 72 and has $200,000. A 4% annual return fits his risk profile. He wants $15,000 at the end of each year for 20 years, with a zero balance at the end. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The sum supports about $14,716 a year, so his goal is not quite realistic
options.B: The sum supports about $16,000 a year, so his goal is realistic
options.C: The sum supports exactly $10,000 a year, so his goal is far too high
options.D: The sum supports about $15,400 a year, so his goal is realistic

questions.rationale: PMT = 200,000 × 0.04 ÷ (1 − 1.04^−20) = $14,716.35. This is less than $15,000. The RR should discuss a lower income, a shorter period or other changes, not more risk.
questions.qa_note: calc: 1.04^-20 = 0.456387; PMT = 8,000 / 0.543613 = 14,716.35. Distractors: 200,000/20 = 10,000; others are invented over-estimates

questions.stem: Rosamund and Piet each invest $100,000 at the same rate for the same term. Each wants equal annual payments that use up the money. Rosamund wants payments at the start of each year. Piet wants them at each year-end. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Their payments are the same, because the sum, rate and term are the same
options.B: Rosamund's payments are smaller, because each payment earns less interest first
options.C: Rosamund's payments are larger, because she receives the money sooner
options.D: Piet's payments are smaller, because his money stays invested for longer

questions.rationale: For the same present value, an annuity due has smaller payments than an ordinary annuity. Each of Rosamund's payments comes one period earlier, so the money earns less interest before it is paid out.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 7.8 exam trap (annuity due payments smaller for same PV)

questions.stem: Benedikt Aalto has a low risk profile and saves for a goal in 15 years. His RR uses a 9% annual return to calculate the deposit that he needs. What is the main problem with this assumption?

options.A: It makes the deposit look too large, so Benedikt saves more than he needs
options.B: It has no effect, because the deposit depends only on the goal and the term
options.C: It makes the deposit look too small and can hide a shortfall
options.D: It is correct, because a long horizon permits the highest historical return

questions.rationale: A higher assumed return reduces the deposit needed. A return that is too high for a low risk profile makes the deposit look small and hides a shortfall. The RR should use realistic after-fee returns that fit the profile.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 7.8 (optimistic rate makes deposit look small and hides a shortfall)

questions.stem: Ottoline Brisebois is a resident of Canada and has never owned a home. She turns 73 this year and wants to open an FHSA. Which statement is correct?

options.A: She cannot open one, because she must be 71 or younger on December 31 of that year
options.B: She can open one, but her contributions are not deductible
options.C: She can open one, because she is a first-time home buyer
options.D: She cannot open one, because she must have earned income in the previous year

questions.rationale: To open an FHSA, a person must be 71 or younger on December 31 of the year that they open it. Being a first-time buyer is not enough. Earned income is not a condition.
questions.source_quote: "You are 71 years or younger as of December 31 of the year you open your FHSA" — research/sources/cra/fhsa-pages.txt CRA FHSA, L106

questions.stem: Mireille Gauthier earned $90,000 in 2025 and belongs to her employer's registered pension plan. Which item reduces the new RRSP room that she gets for 2026?

options.A: Her pension adjustment for 2025
options.B: Her TFSA contributions in 2025
options.C: Her taxable capital gains in 2025
options.D: Her CPP contributions in 2025

questions.rationale: New RRSP room is the lesser of 18% of prior-year earned income and the dollar limit, minus the prior-year pension adjustment. TFSA contributions do not affect RRSP room.
questions.source_quote: "the taxpayer's pension adjustment for the preceding taxation year in respect of an employer" — research/sources/gov/ita-registered-plans-rrsp-tfsa-fhsa-resp.txt ITA s.146(1) RRSP deduction limit, L59

questions.stem: Lorcan Byrne makes an RRSP contribution on February 20, 2027. He has enough deduction room. For which year can he deduct it?

options.A: Only for 2027, the year that he made the contribution
options.B: For 2026, because it is within 60 days after the end of 2026
options.C: Only for 2028, because RRSP deductions apply to the next year
options.D: For any year that he chooses from 2024 to 2027

questions.rationale: A contribution made up to 60 days after the year-end can count for that year. February 20, 2027 is within 60 days after December 31, 2026. He could also choose to deduct it later.
questions.source_quote: "a premium paid by the taxpayer after 1990 and on or before the day that is 60 days after the end of the year under a registered retirement savings plan" — research/sources/gov/ita-registered-plans-rrsp-tfsa-fhsa-resp.txt ITA s.146(5)(a), L97

questions.stem: Annika Sorensen has used all her TFSA room. In March 2026, she withdraws $10,000 from her TFSA. In June 2026, she wants to put the $10,000 back. Which statement is correct?

options.A: She can put it back at any time, because the withdrawal restores her room at once
options.B: She can put it back only after she files her 2026 tax return
options.C: She can never put it back, because TFSA withdrawals permanently reduce her room
options.D: She gets the room back on January 1, 2027, so a June deposit is an excess amount

questions.rationale: A TFSA withdrawal adds the same amount of room on January 1 of the next year. A June 2026 deposit is an excess amount, which is taxed at 1% per month while it stays in the account.
questions.source_quote: "When you withdraw from your TFSA, you will regain the same amount as new available contribution room on January 1 of the following year." — research/sources/cra/tfsa-pages.txt CRA TFSA room, L386

questions.stem: Paloma Reyes contributes $4,000 to an RESP for her daughter this year. Her daughter is eligible for the CESG and has no unused grant room from earlier years. What is the maximum CESG for this contribution?
questions.rationale: The CESG adds 20% of the first $2,500 contributed each year, so the maximum is $500. A grant of $800 would be 20% of the full $4,000. $7,200 is the lifetime maximum.
questions.source_quote: "If eligible, beneficiaries can receive up to 20% of the first $2,500 contributed to the RESP." — research/sources/gov/resp-cesg-clb-esdc-pages.txt ESDC RESP, L158

questions.stem: Florentin Duval lives in Ontario. His son decides not to go to college. Florentin takes the RESP growth as an accumulated income payment. How is this payment taxed?

options.A: At Florentin's regular rate plus an extra 20%
options.B: At his son's regular rate, as an educational assistance payment
options.C: Tax-free, because it is a return of Florentin's contributions
options.D: At Florentin's regular rate plus an extra 12%

questions.rationale: An accumulated income payment is taxed at the subscriber's regular rate plus 20%. The extra rate is 12% only for subscribers in Quebec. Only contributions come back tax-free.
questions.source_quote: "It is taxed at the regular income tax rate of the subscriber, plus an additional 20% (or 12% for subscribers residing in Quebec)." — research/sources/gov/resp-cesg-clb-esdc-pages.txt ESDC RESP, L586

questions.stem: Lionel Okonjo contributed to a spousal RRSP for his wife in 2024 and 2025. She has a low income. She withdraws $20,000 from the plan in 2026. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The withdrawal is always taxed to his wife, because the plan is in her name
options.B: The withdrawal is split equally between Lionel and his wife for tax
options.C: The withdrawal is tax-free, because Lionel already paid tax on the contributions
options.D: Lionel may have to include all or part of the withdrawal in his income

questions.rationale: A contribution to a spousal RRSP in the year of a withdrawal or the two years before can matter. Then the contributor may have to include all or part of the withdrawal in income.
questions.source_quote: "If you contributed to your spouse’s or common law partner’s RRSPs or your spouse’s account under an SPP in 2023, 2024, or 2025, you may have to include in your 2025 income all or part of:" — research/sources/cra/guide-t4040-rrsps-other-registered-plans-retirement-2025.txt T4040 (2025), L3311-3314

questions.stem: Matilda Orrin was 66 on December 31, 2026. She received RRIF income during 2026. Which credit can she claim on that RRIF income?

options.A: The dividend tax credit
options.B: The foreign tax credit
options.C: The pension income amount
options.D: The Canada caregiver amount

questions.rationale: A client can claim the pension income amount on RRIF income if they were 65 or older on December 31 of the year. The dividend tax credit applies to dividends from taxable Canadian corporations, not RRIF income.
questions.source_quote: "You can claim the pension income amount when you receive RRIF income if you were 65 or older on December 31 of the year" — research/sources/cra/rrsp-rrif-hbp-pages.txt CRA RRIF, L782

questions.stem: Tamsin Rourke sells shares of a company at a $4,000 loss. Ten days later, she buys the same shares again for $9,000. She still owns them 30 days after the sale. What is the result?

options.A: She claims the $4,000 loss, and her new shares have an ACB of $9,000
options.B: She claims half of the loss, and her new shares have an ACB of $11,000
options.C: The loss is denied, and her new shares have an ACB of $9,000
options.D: The loss is denied, and her new shares have an ACB of $13,000

questions.rationale: This is a superficial loss, so the loss is denied. Because Tamsin bought the substituted property herself, she can usually add the denied loss to its ACB: $9,000 + $4,000 = $13,000.
questions.source_quote: "However, if you are the person who acquires the substituted property, you can usually add the amount of the superficial loss to the adjusted cost base of the substituted property." — research/sources/cra/capital-gains-losses-superficial-loss-pages.txt CRA, L741

questions.stem: In 2025, Valentin Roux lends $150,000 to his wife at the prescribed rate in effect at that time. She invests it. She pays the interest for 2026 on February 15, 2027. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The income for 2026 is taxed to Valentin, because she paid the interest late
options.B: The income is taxed to his wife, because the loan rate met the prescribed rate
options.C: The income is taxed to his wife, because she paid the interest before her return was due
options.D: The income is split equally, because she paid part of the year late

questions.rationale: The loan exception needs a rate of no less than the prescribed rate. The borrower must also pay each year's interest within 30 days after the year-end. February 15 is more than 30 days late, so attribution applies.
questions.source_quote: "the amount of interest that was payable in respect of the particular year in respect of the loan was paid not later than 30 days after the end of the particular year" — research/sources/gov/ita-attribution-income-splitting.txt ITA s.74.5(2)(b), L84

questions.stem: A CCPC and its associated corporations had adjusted aggregate investment income of $160,000 in the prior year. What is the effect on the CCPC's business limit for the small business deduction this year?

options.A: The business limit is reduced to nil
options.B: The business limit is reduced by $160,000
options.C: The business limit is not affected by investment income
options.D: The business limit is reduced by half, to $250,000

questions.rationale: Each $1 of adjusted aggregate investment income over $50,000 reduces the $500,000 business limit by $5. So the limit is gone at $150,000. At $160,000, the business limit is nil.
questions.source_quote: "D/$500,000 × 5(E − $50,000)" — research/sources/gov/ita-corporate-integration-rdtoh-grip-cda.txt ITA s.125(5.1)(b), L77

questions.stem: A CCPC has a NERDTOH balance from the refundable tax on its investment income. It wants a dividend refund from this balance. Which dividends must it pay?

options.A: Eligible dividends
options.B: Capital dividends
options.C: Non-eligible taxable dividends
options.D: Any dividends, including capital dividends

questions.rationale: Only non-eligible dividends recover NERDTOH. Eligible dividends draw only on ERDTOH. A capital dividend is tax-free and comes from the CDA, so it does not give a dividend refund.
questions.source_quote: "A private corporation’s eligible dividends generate dividend refunds from the ERDTOH. Non-eligible dividends generate dividend refunds from the NERDTOH first, and then possibly from the ERDTOH." — research/sources/cra/guide-t4012-t2-corporation-income-tax-2025.txt T4012 (2025), L8943-8946

questions.stem: A CCPC earns active business income that uses the small business deduction. It pays this income out to its owner as dividends. Which type of dividend normally fits this income?

options.A: Eligible dividends paid from its GRIP
options.B: Non-eligible dividends
options.C: Capital dividends paid from its CDA
options.D: Eligible dividends paid from its ERDTOH

questions.rationale: GRIP reflects income that did not get the small business deduction, so it supports eligible dividends. Small-business income pays non-eligible dividends, with the smaller gross-up and credit. This keeps total tax close to direct earnings.
questions.source_quote: "A CCPC or a deposit insurance corporation may pay eligible dividends to the extent of its GRIP—a balance generally reflecting taxable income that has not benefited from the small business deduction or any other special tax rate" — research/sources/cra/guide-t4012-t2-corporation-income-tax-2025.txt T4012 (2025), L10251-10254

questions.stem: Hamish Calder buys 400 shares at $10 with a $40 commission. Later he buys 600 shares at $15 with a $60 commission. He then sells 300 shares. What is the ACB per share of the 700 shares that remain?
questions.rationale: Average cost includes commissions: (4,040 + 9,060) ÷ 1,000 = $13.10. A sale does not change the average ACB of the shares that remain. $13.00 leaves out the commissions.
questions.qa_note: calc: (400×10+40) + (600×15+60) = 4,040 + 9,060 = 13,100; /1,000 = 13.10. Distractors: simple price average 12.50; simple average incl. commission (10.10+15.10)/2 = 12.60; no commissions 13,000/1,000 = 13.00

questions.stem: In 2025, Odalys Ferreira sells 1,000 shares at $6.50 with a $50 commission. She bought them at $8.00 with a $50 commission. What is her allowable capital loss?
questions.rationale: Capital loss = 6,500 − 8,050 − 50 = −$1,600. At the 2025 inclusion rate of 1/2, the allowable capital loss is $800. $1,600 is the full capital loss before the inclusion rate.
questions.qa_note: calc: proceeds 6,500; ACB 8,000+50 = 8,050; selling expense 50; loss 1,600; × 1/2 = 800. Distractors: one commission ignored 1,550/2 = 775; both ignored 1,500/2 = 750; full loss 1,600

questions.stem: Ingrid Vasquez holds mutual fund trust units with an ACB of $10,000. She receives a $600 return of capital on them. Later she sells all the units for $11,000, with no costs. What is her capital gain?
questions.rationale: A return of capital reduces the ACB to 10,000 − 600 = $9,400. The capital gain is 11,000 − 9,400 = $1,600. $1,000 ignores the return of capital.
questions.qa_note: calc: ACB 10,000 − 600 = 9,400; gain 11,000 − 9,400 = 1,600. Distractors: ROC ignored 1,000; ROC added to ACB 400; ROC added to proceeds 2,200

questions.stem: Desmond Fairweather buys U.S. shares for US$10,000 when US$1 = C$1.30. He sells them for US$11,000 when US$1 = C$1.40. There are no costs. What is his capital gain in Canadian dollars?
questions.rationale: Convert each amount at the rate when it arose. Cost = 10,000 × 1.30 = C$13,000. Proceeds = 11,000 × 1.40 = C$15,400. Gain = C$2,400. C$1,400 converts only the U.S. dollar gain.

questions.stem: Cordelia Hawthorne wants to give $20,000 to a registered charity. She holds listed shares worth $20,000 that have a large accrued gain. Which approach gives the best tax result on the gain?

options.A: Donate the shares directly to the charity
options.B: Sell the shares, then donate the cash proceeds
options.C: Transfer the shares to her RRSP, then donate the cash
options.D: Gift the shares to her spouse, who then sells them

questions.rationale: A donation of listed securities to a qualified donee can get a zero inclusion rate on the gain. If she sells first, the normal inclusion rate applies to the gain.
questions.source_quote: "You may be entitled to an inclusion rate of zero on any capital gain resulting from the donation of any of the following properties to a qualified donee" — research/sources/cra/guide-t4037-capital-gains-2025.txt T4037 (2025), L1045-1047

questions.stem: Fintan Sheehy sells a stock in his RRSP at a $5,000 loss. In the same year, he realizes a $5,000 capital gain in his non-registered account. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The RRSP loss offsets the gain, so he has no taxable capital gain
options.B: Half of the RRSP loss offsets the gain, as an allowable capital loss
options.C: The RRSP loss cannot offset the gain, so the gain is taxable
options.D: The RRSP loss becomes a net capital loss to carry forward

questions.rationale: A client cannot claim a deduction for capital losses within an RRSP. So a loss in the RRSP cannot offset a gain in a non-registered account, and the gain is taxable.
questions.source_quote: "claim a deduction for capital losses within your RRSP" — research/sources/cra/guide-t4040-rrsps-other-registered-plans-retirement-2025.txt T4040 (2025), L1229

questions.stem: Saoirse Kinsella has unused room in both her TFSA and her RRSP. She will buy a growth stock that she expects to sell at a large gain in 10 years. Where should she hold it to minimize tax on the gain?

options.A: In her RRSP, because the withdrawal is taxed at the capital gains inclusion rate
options.B: In her TFSA, because the gain and the withdrawal are generally tax-free
options.C: In a non-registered account, because only part of a capital gain is taxed
options.D: In her RRSP, because the deduction removes all tax on the future gain

questions.rationale: Capital gains in a TFSA are generally tax-free, even on withdrawal. An RRSP only defers tax, and its withdrawals are fully taxable income, so the inclusion-rate advantage is lost.
questions.source_quote: "You generally have to pay tax when you receive payments from the plan." — research/sources/cra/rrsp-rrif-hbp-pages.txt CRA RRSP overview, L12

questions.stem: Leontyne Abbott has 2026 taxable income of $130,000. Use the 2026 federal rates: 14% to $58,523, 20.5% to $117,045 and 26% above. What is her federal tax before credits?
questions.rationale: Each rate applies only to its bracket: 8,193.22 + 11,997.01 + 3,368.30 = $23,558.53. $33,800 applies 26% to all income. $22,846.01 leaves out the 26% bracket.

questions.stem: Isadora Quint is in the 20.5% federal bracket in 2026. She receives a $3,000 non-eligible dividend. The gross-up is 15%. The federal dividend tax credit is 9/13 of the gross-up. What is her federal tax on the dividend?
questions.rationale: Grossed-up dividend = 3,000 × 1.15 = 3,450. Tax = 3,450 × 20.5% = 707.25. Credit = 9/13 × 450 = 311.54. Net tax = $395.71. $707.25 leaves out the credit.

questions.stem: Remy Achterhof is in the 29% federal bracket in 2026. He receives a C$2,000 dividend from a foreign corporation. What is his federal tax on it before any foreign tax credit?
questions.rationale: Foreign dividends get no gross-up and no dividend tax credit. They are taxed in full, like interest: 2,000 × 29% = $580. $385.85 wrongly treats the dividend as an eligible Canadian dividend.
questions.qa_note: calc: 2,000×0.29 = 580. Distractors: eligible treatment 2,760×0.29 − 6/11×760 = 385.85; non-eligible treatment 2,300×0.29 − 9/13×300 = 459.31; gross-up with no credit 2,760×0.29 = 800.40

questions.stem: On September 1, 2025, Aurelie Mbeki buys a 3-year compound GIC. It pays all interest at maturity. What interest must she report on her 2026 tax return?

options.A: No interest, because she receives no cash until 2028
options.B: The interest earned from September 1, 2025 to August 31, 2026
options.C: The interest earned from January 1, 2026 to December 31, 2026
options.D: One third of the total interest that she receives at maturity

questions.rationale: For a multi-year investment, the client reports the interest earned in each complete investment year, from anniversary to anniversary. The first investment year ends on August 31, 2026, so she reports it on her 2026 return.
questions.source_quote: "if you made a long-term investment on July 1, 2024, report the interest earned up to June 30, 2025 on your 2025 return." — research/sources/cra/investment-income-interest-dividends-foreign-tax-credit.txt CRA Line 12100 (2025 tax year), ~L108

questions.stem: Bastien Marchetti has 2026 federal taxable income of $100,000. He earns another $1,000 of interest. At which federal rate is this extra interest taxed?

options.A: 14%, the lowest federal rate
options.B: 20.5%, the rate of his current bracket
options.C: 26%, the next federal rate
options.D: His average federal rate on all income

questions.rationale: Each rate applies only to its bracket. The next dollar of his income falls in the $58,523.01 to $117,045 bracket, so his marginal rate is 20.5%. Interest is fully taxable at the marginal rate.
questions.source_quote: "Provincial or territorial income tax rates apply in addition to federal income tax rates. The tax rates are split up into income brackets. Each rate applies only to the corresponding income bracket, not to all income." — research/sources/cra/tax-rates-brackets-individuals-2025-2026.txt CRA 2026 rates, L13

questions.stem: Philippa Sandoval is 69 and her net income is above the OAS recovery threshold. She replaces $5,000 of interest with $5,000 of eligible dividends. What happens to her net income?

options.A: It stays the same, because she receives the same cash
options.B: It falls, because the dividend tax credit reduces net income
options.C: It rises by $1,900, because $6,900 of grossed-up dividends replaces $5,000 of interest
options.D: It falls by $1,900, because eligible dividends are taxed below interest

questions.rationale: Eligible dividends are grossed up by 38%, so 5,000 × 1.38 = $6,900 goes into net income. The credit reduces tax, not net income. The higher net income can increase her OAS recovery tax.
questions.source_quote: "Multiply the actual amount received by 138% and include the result on line 12000 | Multiply the actual amount received by 115% and include the result on line 12000 and line 12010" — research/sources/cra/investment-income-interest-dividends-foreign-tax-credit.txt CRA lines 12000/12010, L236

questions.stem: Solange Bertrand is in the 20.5% federal bracket in 2026. Which $1,000 of investment income gives her the lowest federal tax? Assume a capital gain has a 1/2 inclusion rate.

options.A: $1,000 of interest from a GIC
options.B: $1,000 of eligible dividends
options.C: $1,000 of non-eligible dividends
options.D: $1,000 of capital gains

questions.rationale: At 20.5%, federal tax is $205 on interest, $131.90 on non-eligible dividends, $102.50 on capital gains and $75.63 on eligible dividends. The eligible dividend has the largest dividend tax credit.

questions.stem: Marcellus Grey emails his dealer. He complains that the call centre made him wait on hold for 40 minutes. He alleges no misconduct. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The dealer must follow its policies for complaints that do not allege misconduct
options.B: The dealer must respond within 90 days, as for any Part E complaint
options.C: The dealer can ignore the email, because it is not a complaint
options.D: The dealer must report it to CIRO, as it does for all complaints

questions.rationale: Part E covers complaints that allege misconduct. Dealers also need policies for complaints that allege no misconduct. A service complaint is not reported to CIRO.
questions.source_quote: "retail client complaints alleging misconduct, and (ii) retail client complaints that do not allege misconduct." — research/sources/ciro/idpc-rules-2026-08-11.txt IDPC 3720(1), L7874-7876

questions.stem: A client tells Esperanza Vidal, an RR, that another RR at the dealer forged her signature. The client makes the complaint verbally. What must Esperanza do?

options.A: Report it to the dealer within two business days
options.B: Report it to the dealer only if the client puts it in writing
options.C: Report it to CIRO directly within five business days
options.D: Report it to the dealer within 90 days

questions.rationale: An Approved Person must report certain complaints about another Approved Person to the dealer within two business days. Forgery is one of these allegations. A complaint in writing or other form is enough.
questions.source_quote: "if the Approved Person becomes aware of a client complaint, in writing or other form, about another Approved Person involving allegations of theft, fraud, misappropriation of funds, securities or other property, forgery, money laundering, market manipulation, insider trading, misrepresentation, or unauthorized trading." — research/sources/ciro/idpc-rules-2026-08-11.txt IDPC 3702(1)(iv), L7658-7661

questions.stem: Gwilym Pryce receives his dealer's final response to his complaint on March 1. He is not satisfied. How long does he have to take his complaint to OBSI?

options.A: 30 days after the final response
options.B: 90 days after the final response
options.C: 180 days after the final response
options.D: Two years after the final response

questions.rationale: A client has 180 days after the dealer's final response to take the complaint to OBSI. The 90-day limit applies to the dealer's response, not to the client.
questions.source_quote: "You have 180 days to bring your complaint to us after the firm has given you a final response." — research/sources/ciro/obsi-how-the-complaint-process-works.txt OBSI how it works, L21

questions.stem: Henrike Vos says that unsuitable advice cost her $500,000. She takes her complaint to OBSI. Which statement about OBSI is correct?

options.A: OBSI can recommend up to $500,000, and the dealer must pay it
options.B: OBSI can recommend up to $350,000, and the dealer must pay it
options.C: OBSI can award any amount, but only after an arbitration hearing
options.D: OBSI can recommend up to $350,000, but its recommendation is not binding

questions.rationale: OBSI can recommend up to $350,000 for a single complaint. Its recommendations are not binding, so the dealer does not have to follow them.
questions.source_quote: "We can recommend up to $350,000 for a single complaint." — research/sources/ciro/obsi-consumer-faqs.txt OBSI FAQ, L48

questions.stem: A dealer resolved a client complaint three years ago. The complaint was not reported to CIRO. How long must the dealer keep a copy of the complaint file?

options.A: Two years from the date of receipt
options.B: Three years from the date of resolution
options.C: Five years from the date of receipt
options.D: Seven years

questions.rationale: The dealer keeps an up-to-date central record for two years from receipt. It must keep a copy of each client complaint file for seven years. Two years is only for the central, readily accessible record.
questions.source_quote: "For each client complaint file, a Dealer Member must maintain a copy for seven years in a location that is retrievable within a reasonable period of time." — research/sources/ciro/idpc-rules-2026-08-11.txt IDPC 3786(2), ~L8052

questions.stem: A dealer's compliance officer sees many complaints over six months about the same switching practice in one branch. What must the dealer do?

options.A: Review its internal procedures and send recommendations to the appropriate management
options.B: Close the complaints, because each one alone is not serious
options.C: Wait until OBSI tells it that the complaints show a serious problem
options.D: Move the RRs in that branch to another branch, then close the files

questions.rationale: Frequent and repeated complaints on similar matters may together show a serious problem. Then the dealer must review its internal procedures and practices. It must also send recommendations to the appropriate management level.
questions.source_quote: "If a Dealer Member determines that the number or severity of complaints is significant, or when a Dealer Member detects frequent and repetitive complaints made with respect to the same or similar matters which may on a cumulative basis indicate a serious problem, the Dealer Member must: (i) review its internal procedures and practices, and (ii) ensure recommendations to remedy the problem are submitted to the appropriate management level." — research/sources/ciro/idpc-rules-2026-08-11.txt IDPC 3723(3)

questions.stem: Oskar Lindqvist is a trader at a Participant. A pension fund client tells him that it will sell 400,000 shares of a thinly traded company. Before Oskar enters the client order, he buys put options on that company for his own account. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Oskar front ran the client order, because a put is a related derivative.
options.B: Oskar did not break UMIR, because front running covers only the same security.
options.C: Oskar made a wash trade, because there was no change in beneficial ownership.
options.D: Oskar did not break UMIR, because he traded for himself and not for the firm.

questions.rationale: Oskar knew of an unentered client order that could affect the price. UMIR 4.1(1) then bars trades in the security or a related derivative. UMIR 10.4 applies this rule to employees. A put is a related derivative, so B is wrong. No exception applies.
questions.source_quote: "market, for the purchase or sale of the security, derivative or any related security or related derivative;" — research/sources/ciro/umir-2026-08-11.txt UMIR 4.1(1)(a), ~lines 5717-5720

questions.stem: Henrike Absalon is an RR. On the trading floor, she hears an unconfirmed rumour that a mining company will receive a takeover bid. She knows of no client order in the stock. She buys the shares for her own account. Under UMIR 4.1, is this front running?

options.A: Yes, because she traded before the takeover bid became public.
options.B: Yes, because any employee trade based on market information is front running.
options.C: No, because she had no knowledge of a specific unentered client order.
options.D: No, because front running applies only to options, not to shares.

questions.rationale: Front running needs knowledge of a specific client order that is not yet entered. UMIR Policy 4.1 says that trading on non-specific market information, including rumours, is not front running. A is wrong because the timing of a public bid is not the UMIR 4.1 test.
questions.source_quote: "Trading based on non-specific pieces of market information, including rumours, does not constitute frontrunning." — research/sources/ciro/umir-2026-08-11.txt UMIR Policy 4.1 Part 2, ~line 5781

questions.stem: Rupert Eskildsen asks his RR to enter a large buy order one minute before the market closes on the last day of the quarter. The order price is well above the last sale price. Rupert wants his quarter-end account value to look higher. Which UMIR concern does this order raise most directly?

options.A: Front running of a client order that is not yet entered
options.B: Trading ahead of a client's expression of interest
options.C: Trading to fix a failed trade before the report is due
options.D: Artificial pricing by setting a high closing price

questions.rationale: UMIR 2.2(2) prohibits orders that could reasonably be expected to create an artificial price. Policy 2.2 lists setting the close as an example. The time of entry and the motive point to an artificial price. A is wrong because there is no other client order to trade ahead of.
questions.source_quote: "effect a high or low closing sale price, ask price or bid price" — research/sources/ciro/umir-2026-08-11.txt UMIR Policy 2.2 Part 2(e)(ii), ~line 4181

questions.stem: Leontyne Abara is an RR. Two accounts of one client often trade the same thinly traded stock with each other. Leontyne believes that the activity may violate UMIR 2.2. What must she do?

options.A: Report the activity to CIRO by the 15th day of the next month
options.B: Watch the accounts for another month to confirm a pattern
options.C: Report the activity forthwith to her supervisor or the compliance department
options.D: Tell the client to stop the trades and record the warning in the file

questions.rationale: Under UMIR 10.16(1), an employee who believes activity may violate a listed rule, such as UMIR 2.2, reports forthwith to a supervisor or compliance. The firm, not the RR, reports findings to CIRO under UMIR 10.16(4). So A is wrong.
questions.source_quote: "shall forthwith report to their supervisor or the compliance department of the Participant upon becoming aware of activity in a principal account, non-client account or client account" — research/sources/ciro/umir-2026-08-11.txt UMIR 10.16(1), ~line 14073

questions.stem: Gideon Mbatha is an RR. A client with a modest stated income makes many cash deposits of about $3,000 each. The client then wires the money abroad. Gideon has reasonable grounds to suspect money laundering, but he cannot prove it. Which statement is correct?

options.A: No report is necessary, because each deposit is below $10,000.
options.B: Gideon must verify the facts before anyone reports to FINTRAC.
options.C: Gideon should ask the client to explain before he escalates the matter.
options.D: The dealer must report the transactions to FINTRAC as soon as practicable.

questions.rationale: PCMLTFA s. 7 requires a report when there are reasonable grounds to suspect money laundering. There is no dollar minimum, and the reporter does not have to verify the facts. Gideon escalates to AML compliance and does not tell the client. So C is wrong.
questions.source_quote: "report to the Centre every financial transaction that occurs or that is attempted in the course of their activities and in respect of which there are reasonable grounds to suspect that" — research/sources/gov/pcmltfa-extracts.txt PCMLTFA s.7, ~lines 77-82

questions.stem: Corentin Abiodun's close friend is the CFO of a listed company. The friend tells Corentin that the company will soon announce a takeover. The news is not public. Corentin asks his RR to buy call options on the company. What should the RR do?

options.A: Decline and report it, because Corentin is a tippee with a material fact
options.B: Accept it, because call options are not securities of the issuer
options.C: Accept it, because only insiders of the issuer are in a special relationship
options.D: Accept it, but put the insider marker 'IA' on the order

questions.rationale: Corentin learned an undisclosed material fact from an officer, so he is a tippee in a special relationship (OSA s. 76(5)). OSA s. 76(6) treats calls as securities of the issuer. UMIR 2.3 bars an order that breaks securities law. A marker does not make the order legal, so D is wrong.
questions.source_quote: "a put, call, option or other right or obligation to purchase or sell securities of the issuer" — research/sources/gov/ontario-securities-act-extracts.txt OSA s.76(6)(a), ~line 437

questions.stem: Ilse Brandvold wants to buy 3,000 shares at $25.00 or less. She accepts any part of the order that fills at once. She wants the unfilled part cancelled immediately. Which order type best meets her needs?

options.A: Fill-or-kill order
options.B: Immediate-or-cancel order
options.C: Iceberg order
options.D: Market order

questions.rationale: An immediate-or-cancel order fills what it can at once and cancels the rest. A fill-or-kill order fills the whole quantity at once or nothing, so it does not accept a partial fill. A market order gives no price control.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 8.3 order table (IOC vs FOK; market terms, not UMIR definitions)

questions.stem: An institutional client wants to buy 300,000 shares of a mid-cap stock during the day. She worries that a large visible order will push the price up. Which order type best addresses her concern?

options.A: A fill-or-kill order for the full quantity
options.B: A market order for the full quantity
options.C: An iceberg order that displays only part of the size
options.D: An immediate-or-cancel order for the full quantity

questions.rationale: An iceberg order displays part of the size, and a hidden reserve refills it. This limits market impact. A market order shows the full demand at once and can fill far from the last price.
questions.source_quote: "disclosed or partially disclosed (i.e., iceberg orders)" — research/sources/ciro/gn-urpart7-26-0007-manipulative-deceptive-trading-practices.txt GN-URPART7-26-0007 Q2.1 'Abusive Liquidity Detection', ~line 94

questions.stem: Wilhelmina Asante holds a volatile small-cap stock that trades at $6.00. She asks for a stop-loss order with a trigger price of $5.40 and no limit price. Which risk should her RR explain?

options.A: The order cancels automatically when the price reaches $5.40.
options.B: The order fills at exactly $5.40, even in a fast market.
options.C: The order becomes a limit order at $5.40 and may never fill.
options.D: The order becomes a market order and may fill well below $5.40.

questions.rationale: A triggered stop-loss order with no limit becomes a market order (GN-URPART7-25-0003). In a fast or thin market, it can fill far from the trigger price. C describes a stop-limit order, which controls the price but may not fill.
questions.source_quote: "entering a stop loss order on a marketplace that, when triggered, will become a "market order"." — research/sources/ciro/gn-urpart7-25-0003-management-of-stop-loss-orders.txt GN-URPART7-25-0003 Q1, ~line 85

questions.stem: Benedikt Osei buys TSX-listed shares in his cash account on a Thursday. The next day, Friday, is a business day. When is the regular settlement date for this trade?

options.A: Thursday, the trade date
options.B: Friday, the next business day
options.C: The following Monday
options.D: The following Tuesday

questions.rationale: Since May 27, 2024, most equity trades settle T+1, the next business day after the trade date (NI 24-101). Monday would be T+2, the former cycle. Tuesday would be T+3.
questions.source_quote: ""T+1" means the next business day following T;" — research/sources/csa/ni-24-101-institutional-trade-matching-and-settlement.txt NI 24-101 s.1.1, ~line 82

questions.stem: Felicity Achterberg sold short 1,000 shares in her margin account. Which change would most likely cause a margin call in her account?

options.A: A fall in the share price
options.B: No change in the share price
options.C: A move of the stock onto the LSERM
options.D: A rise in the share price

questions.rationale: A short position loses value when the price rises. The required credit is (100% + rate) × market value, so a rise increases it and can cause a margin call. A fall in price helps a short seller. Falling prices cause margin calls on long positions.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 8.5 long/short margin table (margin call if the price rises for short)

questions.stem: Ruben Kowalczyk tells his RR to buy 500 shares of a named bank stock today. He lets the RR choose when to enter the order and at what price. Ruben does not have a discretionary account. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The RR may choose the time and price, because Ruben named the security and amount.
options.B: The RR needs a signed discretionary account agreement before entering the order.
options.C: The RR may choose the time and price only after a Supervisor approves each order.
options.D: The RR may also choose a different bank stock, if it gives better execution.

questions.rationale: IDPC 3221(2) exempts time-and-price discretion used for best execution on a client order for a specific amount or a specific security. So Ruben needs no discretionary account. D is wrong because a choice of security is account discretion, which needs a discretionary account.
questions.source_quote: "relating to a client order for a specific amount or a specific security." — research/sources/ciro/idpc-rules-2026-08-11.txt IDPC 3221(2), ~lines 6065-6066

questions.stem: A dealer sends a client a trade confirmation for a purchase of common shares. Which item must the confirmation show?

options.A: The client's risk tolerance from the KYC form
options.B: The RR's share of the commission
options.C: Whether the dealer acted as principal or agent
options.D: The client's total account value after the trade

questions.rationale: IDPC 3816(2) sets the minimum contents of a confirmation. They include whether the dealer acted as principal or agent, the settlement date, the quantity and the consideration. The account statement, not the confirmation, shows the total market value of positions.
questions.source_quote: "whether or not the person or company that executed the trade acted as principal or agent" — research/sources/ciro/idpc-rules-2026-08-11.txt IDPC 3816(2)(i)(c), ~line 9244

questions.stem: Which statement about an Investment Dealer's best execution obligation is correct?

options.A: The dealer must get the best available price on every single client trade.
options.B: The dealer must have best execution policies and review them at least once a year.
options.C: The dealer has no best execution obligation for order-execution-only accounts.
options.D: The dealer must follow all client instructions, even if they break CIRO requirements.

questions.rationale: Best execution is a policies-and-procedures duty. The dealer's policies must address best execution, and the dealer reviews them at least annually (IDPC 3120, 3126). A is wrong because a dealer may not achieve best execution on every single trade. The duty also applies to OEO accounts.
questions.source_quote: "A Dealer Member must review its best execution policies and procedures at least annually" — research/sources/ciro/idpc-rules-2026-08-11.txt IDPC 3126(1), ~line 5269

questions.stem: Desmond Okonkwo wants to buy exactly 4,000 shares of a stock now. He does not want a partial fill. If the full 4,000 shares cannot fill at once, he wants no shares at all. Which order type best meets his needs?

options.A: An iceberg order
options.B: An immediate-or-cancel order
options.C: A stop-limit order
options.D: A fill-or-kill order

questions.rationale: A fill-or-kill order fills the whole quantity at once, or nothing. This is all-or-nothing, as Desmond wants. B is wrong because an immediate-or-cancel order fills what it can at once and cancels the rest, so it can leave a partial fill.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 8.3 order table (FOK: fills the whole quantity at once, or nothing; IOC: fills what it can at once and cancels the rest)

questions.stem: Imogen Thackeray is an RR. A client wants her to trade his account on a discretionary basis. Which condition must Imogen meet before she can trade a discretionary account?

options.A: She must have at least one year of active experience in any one product type.
options.B: She must get the client's verbal approval before she enters each trade.
options.C: She must have at least two years of active experience in all product types traded.
options.D: She must hold the discretionary account at a dealer other than her own dealer.

questions.rationale: IDPC 3275 requires the RR to have at least two years of active experience in trading, advising or analysis for all product types traded. The account must also be at the RR's own dealer, so D is wrong. B describes a non-discretionary account, not a discretionary condition.
questions.source_quote: "has at least two years of active experience in trading, advising or performing analysis with respect to all types of products that are to be traded on a discretionary basis" — research/sources/ciro/idpc-rules-2026-08-11.txt IDPC 3275(1)(i), ~lines 6594-6595

questions.stem: Thaddeus Moravec complains that one of his fills was a few cents worse than a price on another marketplace. His dealer has best execution policies and follows them. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The dealer can meet its duty even if one trade does not get the best price.
options.B: The dealer breached its duty, because every fill must get the best available price.
options.C: The dealer must refund the difference, because best execution guarantees the price.
options.D: The dealer has no best execution duty, because price is not one of the factors.

questions.rationale: Best execution is a policies-and-procedures duty. CIRO says a dealer may not achieve best execution for every single trade. The dealer follows its policies, so one worse fill is not by itself a breach. Price is one of four factors, but the duty does not guarantee the best price on each fill.
questions.source_quote: "may not be able to achieve best execution for every single trade it executes on behalf of a client." — research/sources/ciro/gn-urpart6-25-0003-best-execution-idpc-umir.txt GN-URPART6-25-0003 Q&A, ~line 104

questions.stem: Priya Aaltonen-Reyes tells her dealer to route her order in a way that would cause the dealer to break a CIRO requirement. How must the dealer treat this instruction?

options.A: The dealer must follow it, because client instructions always come first.
options.B: The dealer must not follow the instruction.
options.C: The dealer may follow it if Priya signs a written waiver.
options.D: The dealer may follow it if the order is in an OEO account.

questions.rationale: The dealer must consider client instructions in its best execution process (IDPC 3123). But CIRO says a dealer must not follow client instructions that would cause it to contravene CIRO requirements and securities laws. A waiver or an OEO account does not change this.
questions.source_quote: "a Dealer must not follow client instructions that would cause the Dealer to contravene CIRO requirements and securities laws" — research/sources/ciro/gn-urpart6-25-0003-best-execution-idpc-umir.txt GN-URPART6-25-0003 Q1.3.11, ~line 298

questions.stem: Ignatius Ezeanya has an order-execution-only (OEO) account. He enters his own orders and gets no recommendations. Which statement about best execution for his orders is correct?

options.A: The dealer has no best execution obligation, because it gives no advice.
options.B: Ignatius must find the best marketplace himself, because the account is OEO.
options.C: The dealer keeps its best execution obligation for his orders.
options.D: Best execution applies to his orders only above a set dollar amount.

questions.rationale: CIRO says dealers retain a best execution obligation for orders from a client with an OEO account. The duty does not depend on whether the dealer gives advice. The rule sets no dollar minimum, and the client does not take over the dealer's duty.
questions.source_quote: "Dealers retain a best execution obligation with respect to orders from a client with an order execution only account" — research/sources/ciro/gn-urpart6-25-0003-best-execution-idpc-umir.txt GN-URPART6-25-0003 Q1.4.1, ~line 319

questions.stem: Marisol Venkataraman enters a buy order and a sell order for the same stock at the same time. Both orders are for her own accounts at two dealers. Which term best describes the resulting trade?

options.A: Layering
options.B: Cornering
options.C: Front running
options.D: A wash trade

questions.rationale: A trade with no change in beneficial or economic ownership is a wash trade. Policy 2.2 Part 1 treats it as manipulative by its very nature. Cornering needs trades with the intent of limiting supply. Layering uses non-genuine orders on the other side of the market.
questions.source_quote: "(a) making a fictitious trade; (b) effecting a trade in a security or a derivative which involves no change in the beneficial or economic ownership;" — research/sources/ciro/umir-2026-08-11.txt UMIR Policy 2.2 Part 1(a)-(b), ~lines 4137-4141

questions.stem: Kasimir Adebayo sends many small orders in a stock to find out if a large buyer is present. When he finds one, he buys ahead of that buyer. Which practice is this?

options.A: Quote stuffing
options.B: Layering
options.C: Abusive liquidity detection
options.D: Spoofing

questions.rationale: Abusive liquidity detection uses orders to detect a large buyer or seller, with the intention to trade ahead of that interest. Quote stuffing floods systems with excessive market data messages to get an information advantage. CIRO treats both as manipulative and deceptive practices.
questions.source_quote: "to detect the existence of a large buyer or seller with the intention to trade ahead of, rather than with, the large buyer or seller" — research/sources/ciro/gn-urpart7-26-0007-manipulative-deceptive-trading-practices.txt GN-URPART7-26-0007 Q2.1 'Abusive Liquidity Detection', ~line 94

questions.stem: Leocadia Brunner has $3,000 in her cash account and no other assets at the dealer. She enters an order to buy $250,000 of a stock. She has no reasonable expectation to pay for it. Which UMIR concern does this order raise?

options.A: Front running, because the order is large for the account
options.B: Cornering, because the order limits the supply of the stock
options.C: No concern, because the trade settles on the next business day
options.D: Artificial pricing, because she cannot reasonably expect to pay

questions.rationale: Policy 2.2 Part 2 lists a buy order entered without the ability or the reasonable expectation to make the payment. This activity breaches UMIR 2.2(2). Front running needs knowledge of an unentered client order, and cornering needs the intent of limiting supply.
questions.source_quote: "entering an order for the purchase of a security or a derivative without, at the time of entering the order, having the ability or the reasonable expectation to make the payment" — research/sources/ciro/umir-2026-08-11.txt UMIR Policy 2.2 Part 2(g), ~lines 4189-4191

questions.stem: Tobias Nwachukwu, an RR, enters a client's purchases at successively higher prices to push a stock up. Other sellers absorb the orders, and the price does not change. Did Tobias breach UMIR 2.2(2)?

options.A: Yes, because a listed activity breaches the rule whether or not the price changes.
options.B: No, because no artificial price resulted from the orders.
options.C: No, because the orders were for a client and not for the firm.
options.D: Yes, but only if CIRO proves that he meant to defraud a client.

questions.rationale: Purchases at successively higher prices are a listed activity in Policy 2.2 Part 2. A person who knows or ought reasonably to know of the activity breaches UMIR 2.2(2), irrespective of whether an artificial price results. Client orders are covered, and CIRO need not prove an intent to defraud.
questions.source_quote: "will be in breach of subsection (2) of Rule 2.2 irrespective of whether such activity results in a false or misleading appearance of trading activity" — research/sources/ciro/umir-2026-08-11.txt UMIR Policy 2.2 Part 2 (closing words), ~lines 4217-4219

questions.stem: Esperanza Lindahl, a trader, holds a client buy order. She enters it so that the firm's own buy order at the same price executes first. The client did not consent. Which statement is correct?

options.A: She made a wash trade, because both orders were buy orders.
options.B: She breached UMIR 2.1(2)(c) by seeking priority for the principal order.
options.C: She broke no rule, because both orders were at the same price.
options.D: She committed cornering, because the firm bought before the client.

questions.rationale: Without the client's specific consent, a Participant must not try to get a principal order executed ahead of the client order (UMIR 2.1(2)(c)). A wash trade needs a trade with no change in beneficial ownership, which did not occur here.
questions.source_quote: "without the specific consent of the client, enter client orders and principal orders in such a manner as to attempt to obtain execution of a principal order in priority to the client order" — research/sources/ciro/umir-2026-08-11.txt UMIR 2.1(2)(c), ~lines 3482-3484

questions.stem: Yesterday, Florian Lindgaard's firm agreed to sell a large block to an institution. Today a client gives Florian a large order in the same stock. Florian then enters a principal hedge for the block, sized to its risk, as usual. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The hedge is front running, because Florian now knows of the client order.
options.B: The hedge is allowed only after Florian enters the client order.
options.C: The hedge is allowed, because the firm took on the position before it knew of the client order.
options.D: The hedge is front running, unless the client consents in writing.

questions.rationale: UMIR 4.1(2) allows a principal hedge of a position that the firm agreed to take on before it knew of the client order. The hedge must be commensurate with the risk and follow ordinary practice. Both conditions are met, so the exception applies.
questions.source_quote: "a principal order is entered to hedge a position that the Participant had assumed or agreed to assume before having actual knowledge of the client order" — research/sources/ciro/umir-2026-08-11.txt UMIR 4.1(2)(d), ~lines 5732-5733

questions.stem: Genoveva Park, an RR, receives a large client sell order that could affect the price. Before she enters it, she tells a friend at another firm about it. She does not trade herself. Which statement is correct?

options.A: She did not breach UMIR 4.1, because she did not trade for herself.
options.B: She breached only a duty of confidentiality, not a UMIR rule.
options.C: She did not breach UMIR 4.1, because the friend works at another firm.
options.D: She breached UMIR 4.1, because she told another person before entry.

questions.rationale: UMIR 4.1(1) bars more than trading. Before the client order is entered, a Participant must not inform any other person of it, except in the necessary course of business. A tip to a friend is not in the necessary course of business. UMIR 10.4 applies the rule to Genoveva as an employee.
questions.source_quote: "solicit an order from any other person for the purchase or sale of the security, the derivative, or any related security or related derivative; or (c) inform any other person, other than in the necessary course of business, of the client order." — research/sources/ciro/umir-2026-08-11.txt UMIR 4.1(1)(b)-(c), ~lines 5721-5724

questions.stem: A dealer's investigation finds that a client account made a wash trade in breach of UMIR. The violation happened only once, and the amount was small. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The dealer need not report it, because it happened only once.
options.B: The dealer must still report the finding to CIRO.
options.C: The dealer must report it only if the client made a profit.
options.D: The dealer need not report it, because the amount was small.

questions.rationale: Under UMIR 10.16(4), the dealer reports a finding of a UMIR violation to CIRO. CIRO expects the report even if the investigation concludes that the violation occurred only once. The rule has no profit test and no dollar test.
questions.source_quote: "even if the investigation concludes that the violation has occurred only once" — research/sources/ciro/gn-urpart10-26-0003-gatekeeper-reporting-obligation.txt GN-URPART10-26-0003 Q2.7, ~line 153

questions.stem: Horatio Ilunga's RR escalated his unusual cash deposits to AML compliance. Horatio asks the RR if the dealer will report him to FINTRAC. What should the RR do?

options.A: Confirm the report, so that he can explain the deposits
options.B: Tell him that reports apply only above $10,000
options.C: Not tell him about any possible report
options.D: Ask him to sign a consent before any report

questions.rationale: FINTRAC guidance says not to tip off the client about a suspicious transaction report. Disclosure of a report to prejudice a criminal investigation is also an offence (PCMLTFA s. 8). Suspicious transaction reports have no dollar threshold, and the dealer needs no client consent.
questions.source_quote: "It is important to not tip off your client about the fact that you are filing a Suspicious Transaction Report" — research/sources/gov/fintrac-str-guidance.txt FINTRAC STR guidance, ~line 147

questions.stem: Ingrid Valdivieso is an RR. A client's $600 transaction gives her reasonable grounds to suspect terrorist financing. A colleague says that the amount is too small to report. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The dealer need not report it, because it is below $10,000.
options.B: The dealer must report it only after a second similar transaction.
options.C: The dealer need not report it until it has proof of an offence.
options.D: The dealer must report it, because suspicious transaction reports have no dollar threshold.

questions.rationale: There is no monetary threshold for a suspicious transaction report. The test is reasonable grounds to suspect a link to money laundering, terrorist financing or sanctions evasion. The dealer does not have to verify the facts or prove an offence.
questions.source_quote: "There is no monetary threshold associated with the reporting of a suspicious transaction." — research/sources/gov/fintrac-str-guidance.txt FINTRAC STR guidance, ~line 239

questions.stem: Jovan Mukherjee wants to deposit a large bank draft. When his RR asks about the source of funds, Jovan gives a vague answer and cancels the deposit. The RR has reasonable grounds to suspect money laundering. Which statement is correct?

options.A: The dealer must report the attempted transaction to FINTRAC.
options.B: No report is needed, because the deposit did not occur.
options.C: The dealer must report it only if Jovan tries the deposit again.
options.D: The RR must ask Jovan to complete the deposit before any report.

questions.rationale: PCMLTFA s. 7 requires a report of every financial transaction that occurs or that is attempted, if there are reasonable grounds to suspect. The cancelled deposit is an attempted transaction, so it is reportable. A second attempt is not a condition.
questions.source_quote: "report to the Centre every financial transaction that occurs or that is attempted in the course of their activities and in respect of which there are reasonable grounds to suspect that" — research/sources/gov/pcmltfa-extracts.txt PCMLTFA s.7, ~lines 77-82

questions.stem: Kalinda Sorensen, an RR, has reasonable grounds to suspect that a client's trades relate to money laundering. She reports the trades to her superior, as the dealer's procedures require. Which statement about Kalinda is correct?

options.A: She must also file her own separate report directly with FINTRAC.
options.B: She has a defence, because she reported the transaction to her superior.
options.C: She commits an offence unless she also tells the client.
options.D: She has a defence only after the dealer files the report.

questions.rationale: Under PCMLTFA s. 75(2), an employee who reports a suspicious transaction to a superior has a defence. The defence comes from her own report to the superior, not from the dealer's later filing. Telling the client would be a tip-off, which FINTRAC guidance says to avoid.
questions.source_quote: "No employee of a person or an entity shall be convicted of an offence under subsection (1) in respect of a transaction or proposed transaction that they reported to their superior" — research/sources/gov/pcmltfa-extracts.txt PCMLTFA s.75(2), ~line 144

questions.stem: Lucian Ogunwale is an officer of a listed company. He tells his brother about a merger that is not yet public. He does not tell him in the necessary course of business. The brother does not trade. Which statement is correct?

options.A: No breach occurred, because no securities were bought or sold.
options.B: Only the brother breached the law, because he received the fact.
options.C: Lucian breached OSA s. 76(2), even though no one traded.
options.D: No breach occurred, because the brother is a family member.

questions.rationale: A person in a special relationship must not tell others an undisclosed material fact. The only exception is the necessary course of business (OSA s. 76(2)). As an officer, Lucian is in a special relationship. The tip itself is the breach, so no trade is needed.
questions.source_quote: "No issuer and no person or company in a special relationship with an issuer shall inform, other than in the necessary course of business, another person or company of a material fact or material change" — research/sources/gov/ontario-securities-act-extracts.txt OSA s.76(2), ~line 403

questions.stem: On a train, Nikolai Esposito overhears two strangers discuss a possible takeover of a listed company. He has no way to know who they are or how they learned it. Is Nikolai in a special relationship with the issuer?

options.A: Yes, because anyone who learns of a takeover is a tippee.
options.B: Yes, because a takeover is always a material fact.
options.C: No, because only insiders and employees can be in a special relationship.
options.D: No, because he cannot reasonably know that his source is in a special relationship.

questions.rationale: A tippee is in a special relationship only if they know, or ought to know, that their source is in one. Nikolai cannot know this. The special relationship is not limited to insiders and employees. It also covers tippees and persons who do business with the issuer.
questions.source_quote: "knows or ought reasonably to have known that the other person or company is a person or company in such a relationship" — research/sources/gov/ontario-securities-act-extracts.txt OSA s.76(5)(e), ~line 434

questions.stem: UMIR 6.2 requires an 'IA' or 'SS' marker on some orders. What is the main purpose of these markers?

options.A: To help regulators find possible insider trading
options.B: To give these orders priority over other client orders
options.C: To show that the order is a short sale
options.D: To exempt these orders from best execution

questions.rationale: UMIR 6.2 requires a marker on an order for the account of an insider (IA) or a significant shareholder (SS). CIRO says these markers help regulators identify possible insider trading. A short sale has its own short-sale marker.
questions.source_quote: "These markers help securities regulators identify potential violations of securities laws, specifically related to insider trading." — research/sources/ciro/gn-urpart6-26-0004-insider-significant-shareholder-markers.txt GN-URPART6-26-0004 s.1.1, ~line 71

questions.stem: Pascal Ruangsri has information about a market manipulation scheme at his employer. He wants to report it and be eligible for a financial award. Which program should he use?

options.A: The CIRO Whistleblower Service
options.B: The OSC Whistleblower Program
options.C: A FINTRAC suspicious transaction report
options.D: An internal report under UMIR 10.16

questions.rationale: The OSC Whistleblower Program can pay an award of 5% to 15% of sanctions and/or voluntary payments, to a maximum of $5 million. The CIRO Whistleblower Service treats tips in confidence, but it offers no financial award. Internal and FINTRAC reports carry no award.
questions.source_quote: "The amount of an award ranges from 5% to 15% of the total monetary sanctions ordered by the Commission" — research/sources/csa/osc-whistleblower-program-web-pages.txt OSC whistleblower pages, ~line 201

questions.stem: Quintessa Moyo reports a suspected securities law breach by her employer to the OSC. Two weeks later, her employer demotes her. She starts a court action for reprisal. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Quintessa must prove that the demotion was a reprisal.
options.B: The protection applies only if she reported internally first.
options.C: The employer must prove that the demotion was not a reprisal.
options.D: No protection applies, because a demotion is not a dismissal.

questions.rationale: OSA s. 121.6 protects a report to the OSC, and a reprisal includes a demotion. In a court action or arbitration, the employer has the burden of proof that it took no reprisal. The law does not require an internal report first.
questions.source_quote: "the burden of proof that the person or company did not take a reprisal against a specified individual in contravention of subsection (2) lies on that person or company" — research/sources/gov/ontario-securities-act-extracts.txt OSA s.121.6(6), ~line 516

questions.stem: Rasmus Montclair opened an account to save for retirement with modest monthly deposits. Six months later, large wires arrive from several unrelated third parties and leave within days. What does CIRO expect the dealer to do?

options.A: Close the account at once, without any review
options.B: Take no action, because the KYC form is already on file
options.C: Report the activity to CIRO as a UMIR 10.16 finding
options.D: Investigate further, because the activity does not match the stated use

questions.rationale: CIRO expects the recorded intended use of an account to be consistent with the client's KYC and transactions. If it is not, the dealer should investigate further. UMIR 10.16 deals with UMIR breaches such as manipulation. Suspected money laundering goes to FINTRAC.
questions.source_quote: "If not, the Investment Dealer should conduct further investigation." — research/sources/ciro/gn-3200-23-001-aml-compliance-guidance.txt GN-3200-23-001 s.5.1.2, ~line 421

questions.stem: Saoirse Abubakar wants to buy 800 shares of a stock that trades near $41. She will pay no more than $40. She accepts that the order may not fill. Which order type fits her needs?

options.A: A limit order at $40
options.B: A market order
options.C: A buy stop order at $40
options.D: A fill-or-kill order at the market

questions.rationale: A limit order buys at no more than a set maximum price. It gives price control, but it may not fill. A market order buys at the best ask on entry, so she would pay about $41. A buy stop sits above the market, not below it.
questions.source_quote: "buy a security or derivative to be executed at a specified maximum price" — research/sources/ciro/umir-2026-08-11.txt UMIR 1.1 'limit order' (a), ~line 1553

questions.stem: Tiberius Strandqvist wants to sell 6,000 shares of a thinly traded stock at once. He asks for a market order. Which risk should his RR explain?

options.A: The order may not fill at all, even when buyers are present.
options.B: The order may fill at prices well below the last sale price.
options.C: The order will fill only at the last sale price or better.
options.D: The order will be cancelled if it cannot fill in full.

questions.rationale: A market order sells at the best bid on entry. It gives certainty of execution, but not of price. In a thin market, it can fill far from the last price. A limit order, not a market order, carries the risk of no fill.
questions.source_quote: "sell a security or a derivative to be executed upon entry to a marketplace at the best bid price." — research/sources/ciro/umir-2026-08-11.txt UMIR 1.1 'market order' (b), ~line 1634

questions.stem: Ulrike Mensah sold short 1,000 shares at $30. She wants to limit her loss if the price rises sharply. Which order best meets her goal?

options.A: A sell stop order with a trigger at $27
options.B: A buy limit order at $27
options.C: A buy stop order with a trigger at $33
options.D: A sell limit order at $33

questions.rationale: A short seller loses money when the price rises. A buy stop sits above the market and, at the trigger, becomes an order to buy back the shares. A sell stop sits below the market and protects a long position. A buy limit at $27 fills only if the price falls.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 8.3 order table (stop orders: sell stops below the market, buy stops above; short sale loss on a rise)

questions.stem: Viggo Takahashi holds a stock at $22. He has a stop-limit sell order with a $20 trigger and a $19.50 limit. After bad news, the stock opens at $17. What most likely happens?

options.A: The order fills at $17, because the price reached the trigger.
options.B: The order fills at $20, because that is the trigger price.
options.C: The order fills at $19.50, because the limit price is guaranteed.
options.D: The order triggers but does not fill, because the price is below the limit.

questions.rationale: At the trigger, a stop-limit order becomes a limit order to sell at $19.50 or better. The price fell past the limit in one jump, so the order may not fill. A stop-loss order with no limit would become a market order and could fill near $17.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 8.3 on-stop orders (stop-limit controls price but may not fill if the price jumps past the limit)

questions.stem: A dealer allows market stop-loss orders only when CIRO's conditions are met. Which client order meets all of them?

options.A: A very liquid, low-volatility stock; trigger near the market; normal order size
options.B: A very liquid, low-volatility stock; trigger far below the market; normal order size
options.C: A thinly traded, low-volatility stock; trigger near the market; normal order size
options.D: A very liquid, low-volatility stock; trigger near the market; size ten times average

questions.rationale: CIRO lists three conditions for a market stop-loss order. The security is very liquid, with relatively low historic volatility. The trigger is near the market at entry. The size is not much greater than the average trade size. Each other order fails one condition.
questions.source_quote: "the use should be limited to orders for the purchase or sale of a particular security which meets all of the following conditions" — research/sources/ciro/gn-urpart7-25-0003-management-of-stop-loss-orders.txt GN-URPART7-25-0003 Q1, ~line 100

questions.stem: Wanjiru Kaarlsen's RR says that her short sale can execute only at or above the last sale price. Is the RR correct?

options.A: Yes, because UMIR 3.2 still contains this price test.
options.B: No, because that restriction was repealed effective October 15, 2012.
options.C: Yes, but only for a Short Sale Ineligible Security.
options.D: No, because a short sale must execute below the last sale price.

questions.rationale: The former rule allowed a short sale only at or above the last sale price. It was repealed effective October 15, 2012, so there is no tick test. A Short Sale Ineligible Security cannot be sold short at all. No rule requires a price below the last sale.
questions.source_quote: "approved amendments to repeal Rule 3.1 and Policy 3.1 effective October 15, 2012." — research/sources/ciro/umir-2026-08-11.txt UMIR Rule 3.1 regulatory history, ~line 5180

questions.stem: Xavier Ndiaye wants to sell short a TSX stock in his margin account. The stock is not a Pre-Borrow Security or a Short Sale Ineligible Security. Which steps does UMIR require before entry?

options.A: Arrange to borrow the shares, then mark the order short.
options.B: Mark the order short and set a price at or above the last sale.
options.C: Mark the order short and have a reasonable expectation to settle.
options.D: Get Market Regulator approval, then mark the order short.

questions.rationale: UMIR 3.2 requires a short-sale marker, and UMIR 3.3 requires a reasonable expectation to settle. A borrowing arrangement before entry is required only for a Pre-Borrow Security. The last-sale-price test was repealed in 2012.
questions.source_quote: "if the security is a Pre-Borrow Securit y, unless the Participant or Access Person has made arrangements for the borrowing" — research/sources/ciro/umir-2026-08-11.txt UMIR 3.2(1)(c), ~line 5442 (corpus extraction splits the word as "Securit y"; quoted as extracted)

questions.stem: Yolanda Kristiansen asks how an alternative trading system (ATS) differs from an exchange. Which statement is correct?

options.A: An ATS lists issuers, but it has no power to discipline its subscribers.
options.B: An ATS is not a marketplace, so UMIR does not apply to its trades.
options.C: An ATS can trade only securities that no exchange lists.
options.D: An ATS does not list issuers, and it disciplines subscribers only by exclusion.

questions.rationale: Under NI 21-101, an exchange lists issuers and disciplines its members. An ATS does not list issuers, and it disciplines subscribers only by exclusion from the marketplace. An ATS is one of the four types of marketplace, so its trades are marketplace trades.
questions.source_quote: "discipline subscribers other than by exclusion from participation in the marketplace" — research/sources/csa/ni-21-101-marketplace-operation.txt NI 21-101 s.1.1 'alternative trading system' (a)(ii)(D), ~lines 34-35

questions.stem: Zbigniew Afolabi, an RR, has one client who wants to sell a TSX-listed stock and another who wants to buy it. He suggests that they trade privately at an agreed price. No exemption applies. What does UMIR require?

options.A: The trade must occur by entry of an order on a marketplace.
options.B: The trade may occur privately if both clients sign a consent.
options.C: The trade may occur privately if the price is the last sale price.
options.D: The trade must occur through the dealer's own inventory account.

questions.rationale: UMIR 6.4 says that, unless an exemption applies, a trade must occur by the entry of an order on a marketplace. Client consent or a fair price does not create an exemption. Use of another person to trade off a marketplace without an exemption also breaches UMIR 2.1(2)(a).
questions.source_quote: "may not trade nor participate in a trade in a security by means other than the entry of an order on a marketplace." — research/sources/ciro/umir-2026-08-11.txt UMIR 6.4(1), ~line 7579

questions.stem: Anneliese Vukovic enters a limit order to buy at $15.00. An hour later, she phones her RR and changes the limit to $15.25. What must the dealer's order record show?

options.A: Only the final terms, because the first order did not fill
options.B: The original terms and the change to the limit price
options.C: Only the original terms, because a change needs a new order ticket
options.D: Nothing until the order fills, because open orders need no record

questions.rationale: IDPC 3815(1) requires a record of each order, executed or unexecuted. The record shows the terms of the order and of any modification or cancellation. So the record must show both the original limit and the change.
questions.source_quote: "the terms and conditions of the order, transaction or instruction and of any modification or cancellation thereof," — research/sources/ciro/idpc-rules-2026-08-11.txt IDPC 3815(1)(i), ~line 9200

questions.stem: Barnaby Chukwu asks his RR to buy 500 shares. The RR enters 5,000 shares by mistake, and the order fills. How may the dealer correct the error?

options.A: Leave all 5,000 shares in the account, because the trade is final
options.B: Cross the extra shares with another client off a marketplace
options.C: Adjust the error by a journal entry, without a new marketplace trade
options.D: Cancel the trade and keep no record of the error

questions.rationale: UMIR 6.4 lets a dealer adjust by a journal entry an error in connection with a client order. Crosses off a marketplace need an exemption. Supervision watches for excessive transfers and cancellations, so the dealer keeps a record of the correction.
questions.source_quote: "to adjust by a journal entry an error in connection with a client order;" — research/sources/ciro/umir-2026-08-11.txt UMIR 6.4(2)(c), ~line 7592

questions.stem: Dariusz Krzyzanowski often buys and sells US-listed stocks. He holds only a CAD account at his dealer. Which statement about opening a USD account is correct?

options.A: It removes all currency risk on his US-dollar holdings.
options.B: It avoids repeated currency conversions, but not currency risk.
options.C: It means that the dealer charges no spread on any conversion.
options.D: It removes the best execution duty on his US trades.

questions.rationale: In a CAD account, each USD trade converts at the dealer's rate, which includes a spread. A USD account avoids repeated conversions. But the holdings stay in US dollars, so their CAD value still moves with the exchange rate.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 8.4 FX (USD account avoids repeated conversions but not currency risk; conversions include a dealer spread)

questions.stem: Eulalia Grimsson's cash-account purchase is unpaid 22 business days after settlement date. She pays half of the balance. She then asks to buy a new stock in the same account. Can the RR enter the order?

options.A: Yes, because her partial payment lifts the restriction.
options.B: Yes, because the restriction applies only to her other accounts.
options.C: No, because part of the balance is still 20 or more business days overdue.
options.D: Yes, because the restriction starts only at 30 business days.

questions.rationale: When any portion of a cash-account money balance is outstanding 20 business days or more after settlement date, the client can enter only liquidating transactions. Half the balance is still overdue, so the restriction stays. It covers any account of the client.
